choices: Reinstall VS Code — the keybinding is broken
Use Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) to open the Command Palette and type the command — every command is reachable by name
The feature doesn't exist — the menu bar is the only way
Edit keybindings.json to add every command manually
evidence: # developer hunting through 6 levels of menus for 'Fold All'
scenarios.hint: What's the one shortcut that finds any command by typing its name?
scenarios.prompt: What is the keyboard-first way to run any command?
scenarios.situation: A developer digs through nested menus to find 'Fold All'.
scenarios.title: Hunting through menus
scenarios.why: The Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) is VS Code's universal command launcher: type a few letters of any command — menu items, extension actions, settings — and run it without touching the mouse. Ctrl+P is its sibling for quick file opening. Keyboard-first navigation compounds: the palette removes the need to memorize dozens of individual shortcuts.

choices: Add a launch.json configuration with type, request, and program fields — the debugger needs to know what to launch and how
Debugging works without configuration — just press F5
Install a separate debugger application — VS Code can't debug
launch.json is only for Node.js — Python needs a different file
evidence:
# settings.json exists; no launch.json
# F5 prompts: 'select a debug configuration'
scenarios.hint: F5 asks for a configuration. What file defines debug configurations — and what three fields describe 'launch this program'?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and what goes in it?
scenarios.situation: Pressing F5 prompts to select a debug configuration; none exists.
scenarios.title: F5 with nowhere to go
scenarios.why: launch.json in .vscode/ defines debug configurations: type (debugger, e.g. node/python), request (launch vs attach), program (what to run), plus args, env, and preLaunchTask. F5 then starts a real debug session with breakpoints. Without it, VS Code doesn't know what 'debug' means for this project — the prompt is the editor asking you to define it.

choices: Select each occurrence with the mouse — precision matters
Use Ctrl+D (Cmd+D) to select the next occurrence, or Alt+Click for multiple cursors — edit all occurrences simultaneously
Find-and-replace across the file is the only safe way
Multi-cursor doesn't exist in VS Code — use an online tool
evidence: // rename `userId` to `accountId` in 12 places in this file
scenarios.hint: You want 12 carets, one per occurrence, typing once. What adds the next occurrence to the selection?
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest in-file rename?
scenarios.situation: A variable must be renamed in 12 places within one file.
scenarios.title: Twelve edits, one keystroke
scenarios.why: Ctrl+D selects the next occurrence of the current selection, adding a cursor each time (with skip via Ctrl+K Ctrl+D); then typing edits all simultaneously. Alt+Click places cursors arbitrarily. For cross-file renames, F2 (rename symbol) is the language-aware tool — multi-cursor is for the local, mechanical case. The pattern: let the editor multiply your keystrokes.

choices: User settings apply everywhere and can't be overridden
Workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json) override user settings for that project — commit the workspace file so the team shares formatting
Settings can't be shared — everyone configures manually
The team must use the same OS for settings to apply
scenarios.hint: Two levels: your personal defaults, and the project's. Which one should the repo carry so every clone formats identically?
scenarios.prompt: How should formatting be standardized across the team?
scenarios.situation: Inconsistent formatting across the team; some have format-on-save, some don't.
scenarios.title: Everyone formats differently
scenarios.why: VS Code settings layer: user settings (personal defaults) < workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json, committed). Committing the workspace file makes format-on-save, the formatter choice, and rulers consistent for every clone — the repo carries its own editor contract. Personal preferences stay in user settings; project requirements go in the workspace file.

choices: Type the Emmet abbreviation and press Tab — e.g. ul>li.item*5 expands to the full list
Write all the HTML by hand — abbreviations are unreliable
Emmet only works in .html files — not in JSX
Install a separate Emmet extension — it's not built in
scenarios.hint: `ul>li.item*5` is a tiny language for HTML structure. What key expands it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you generate the markup quickly?
scenarios.situation: A developer hand-writes repetitive HTML lists.
scenarios.title: The unexpanded abbreviation
scenarios.why: Emmet is built into VS Code: CSS-like abbreviations (ul>li.item*5, div.container>header+main+footer) expand with Tab into full markup, including numbering ($), attributes, and lorem text. It works in HTML, JSX, and more. Hand-writing repetitive structure is the slowest possible approach to a solved problem.

choices: Reload the window — the extension activates eventually
Check the extension's requirements: many language extensions need a language server binary, SDK, or runtime installed separately (e.g., Python interpreter, .NET SDK)
Extensions always work out of the box — the code must be wrong
Uninstall and reinstall VS Code — the extension host is corrupted
evidence: # installed 'Python' extension; no IntelliSense, no 'Run Python File'
scenarios.hint: The extension is a client; who does the actual language work — and is that piece installed?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the extension inert?
scenarios.situation: A language extension installs but provides no features.
scenarios.title: The extension that does nothing
scenarios.why: Most language extensions are front-ends for a language server, SDK, or runtime that must exist separately — the Python extension needs a Python interpreter selected, C# needs the .NET SDK, Java needs a JDK. The extension contributes UI; the toolchain does the work. First check in the extension's docs: 'Requirements'. Installing the UI without the engine is the classic empty-extension experience.

scenarios.title: The menu spelunker
scenarios.situation: A developer hunts through five levels of menus for 'Fold All' — twice a day. They know VS Code can do it; they re-find it every time. (Companion to the existing scenario 'Hunting through menus.')
evidence: Observed: A developer hunts through five levels of menus for 'Fold All' — twice a day. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use the command palette (2) Discover commands by search Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct command-palette workflow?
choices: A. Memorize the menu tree; the structure is the documentation.

B. Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P as the universal interface: every command searchable by fuzzy name ('fold all'), recent commands ranked first, keybinding shown beside each result — the menu becomes a search box; the twice-daily hunt becomes 2 seconds of typing.
C. The menu is fine; hunting builds familiarity.
D. Bind everything; the palette is for beginners.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the developer re-finds 'Fold All' twice daily. What finds commands by name?
scenarios.why: The command palette inverts command discovery: instead of navigating the menu tree to the command, you name the command and the palette finds it — fuzzy-matched, with the keybinding displayed so the frequent ones graduate to muscle memory. The recent-first ranking means the twice-daily 'Fold All' surfaces after typing 'fo'. Binding everything (choice D) doesn't scale to 500 commands; the palette is the interface for the long tail, and the displayed keybindings teach the shortcuts for the head. The menu hunt was a retrieval problem; the palette is the retrieval tool.

scenarios.title: The twelve-edit chore
scenarios.situation: A developer renames a CSS class across 12 spots in one file — find-replace dialog, carefully scoped, twice (once for the HTML). A colleague does it with multi-cursors in 20 seconds. (Companion to the existing scenario 'Twelve edits, one keystroke.')
evidence: Observed: A developer renames a CSS class across 12 spots in one file — find-replace dialog, carefully scoped, twice (once for the HTML). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Edit with multi-cursors (2) Select occurrences incrementally Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct multi-cursor technique?
choices: A. Find-replace dialog; the scoping is safer.

B. Add cursors semantically: Ctrl/Cmd+D selects the next occurrence (each press adds one), Alt+click places cursors manually, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+L selects all occurrences — then type once; the 12 edits happen in one keystroke, each visible as you go.
C. Multi-cursor is a party trick; the dialog is the tool.
D. Edit each occurrence; precision matters.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the colleague's 12 edits were visible as they happened. What shows every edit live?
scenarios.why: Multi-cursors turn N edits into one: each cursor is a live editing point, and typing happens at all of them simultaneously — with every occurrence visible, so the 'careful scoping' the dialog needed is replaced by sight. Ctrl+D's incremental selection is the control: each press adds the next occurrence, so you watch the set grow and stop before the false positive — safer than the dialog's blind Replace All. Alt+click handles the irregular cases (the occurrences that aren't textually identical). The 20-second colleague wasn't showing off; they were using the editor's native parallelism — the dialog is the serial fallback.

choices: Use find-and-replace across the project — fastest
Place the caret on the symbol and press Shift+F6 (Rename refactoring) — updates all references safely, respecting scope
Rename the file — the class follows automatically
Rename only the declaration — references update themselves
scenarios.hint: Find-and-replace can't tell a class name from a comment containing the same word. What refactoring understands scope and references?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rename?
scenarios.situation: A class used in 40 files must be renamed.
scenarios.title: Renaming across forty files
scenarios.why: Shift+F6 Rename is a language-aware refactoring: it updates declarations, references, and (optionally) related files while respecting scope — a comment mentioning the old name isn't touched, a shadowing local isn't renamed. Find-and-replace is textual and blind. The IDE's refactoring engine exists precisely so renames are safe, previewable operations, not hope-driven edits.

choices: Open the file in the editor first — there's no global search
Press Shift twice (Search Everywhere) or Ctrl+Shift+F (Find in Path) — search classes, files, symbols, and text across the project
Use the OS file search — the IDE can't search contents
Grep in the terminal — the IDE has no search
evidence: # where is `calculateTax` defined? which files reference the `discount` field?
scenarios.hint: You need to find a symbol by name and text across the whole project. What searches everything — files, classes, actions — from one box?
scenarios.prompt: How do you locate the symbol and its usages?
scenarios.situation: A developer browses the project tree looking for a method definition.
scenarios.title: Browsing instead of searching
scenarios.why: Search Everywhere (double-Shift) finds classes, files, symbols, and IDE actions by name; Find in Path (Ctrl+Shift+F) searches file contents with regex and scope filters; Alt+F7 finds usages of the symbol at the caret. Tree-browsing is linear; search is indexed. Professional IDE fluency is largely navigation fluency.

choices: Add print statements — the debugger is too slow for this
Set a breakpoint (Ctrl+F8), run in Debug mode, and use Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) plus Watches to inspect state — no code changes needed
The debugger can't inspect variables — only the console can
Restart the app with more logging and redeploy
evidence: # intermittent wrong total in a 200-line calculation; prints would take hours
scenarios.hint: You need to see variable values at a specific line, on demand, without editing code. What pauses execution and lets you interrogate state?
scenarios.prompt: What is the efficient approach?
scenarios.situation: An intermittent wrong total in a long calculation; print-debugging would take hours.
scenarios.title: Interrogating the running program
scenarios.why: The debugger pauses at breakpoints and lets you inspect the full state: Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) runs arbitrary expressions in the current frame, Watches track values across steps, and conditional breakpoints stop only on the failing case. Print-debugging edits code, rebuilds, and reruns per hypothesis — the debugger tests hypotheses in seconds without touching the source.

choices: Delete the method and rewrite it — extraction is manual
Select the block and use Extract Method (Ctrl+Alt+M) — the IDE creates the method, infers parameters and return, and replaces the block with a call
Copy-paste into a new method and fix the references by hand
Long methods are fine — extraction hurts readability
evidence: // 60-line method; a 15-line block is copy-pasted in 3 places
scenarios.hint: The IDE can carve a method out of selected code. What does it infer — parameters in, value out?
scenarios.prompt: How should the duplication be removed?
scenarios.situation: A 15-line block is duplicated in three places inside a long method.
scenarios.title: The tripled block
scenarios.why: Extract Method (Ctrl+Alt+M) analyzes the selection, infers parameters (values read) and return (value written), creates the method, and replaces each copy with a call. Manual extraction risks missing a variable or mis-wiring a parameter; the refactoring is provably behavior-preserving. Duplicated blocks are the canonical extract-method trigger.

choices: Run configurations are fixed — one per project
Create a run configuration (Run > Edit Configurations) with the right main class/script, arguments, and environment — configurations are shareable via .run/ or versioned files
The IDE always runs the currently open file — that's the only option
Run configurations can't take arguments — hardcode them
evidence: # app needs --port 8081 and ENV=staging to run locally
scenarios.hint: Running needs more than 'press play': arguments, env vars, working directory. Where does the IDE store a named, repeatable launch?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the launch repeatable?
scenarios.situation: Local runs need specific args and env vars; the developer retypes them each time.
scenarios.title: Retyping the launch
scenarios.why: Run configurations capture the launch recipe — main class/script, program arguments, environment variables, working directory — as a named, one-click (and debuggable) entry. They can be shared with the team via versioned files. Retyping args per launch is slow and error-prone; the configuration makes 'how do I run this' a stored answer.

choices: Press Alt+Enter on the warning — intention actions offer the fix (add import, create method, suppress with justification) right at the caret
Ignore all warnings — they're just style opinions
Warnings can't be fixed in bulk — each needs manual editing
Disable inspections entirely — they slow down the IDE
evidence: // IDE highlights: 'Method can be static', 'Unused import', 'Possible NPE'
scenarios.hint: The IDE already knows what's wrong — and usually knows the fix. What key asks it 'what can you do here?'
scenarios.prompt: How should the warnings be handled?
scenarios.situation: The IDE highlights several warnings; the developer isn't sure what to do about them.
scenarios.title: The yellow squiggles
scenarios.why: Alt+Enter (Show Intention Actions) is the IDE's 'fix it for me' key: it offers the applicable quick-fix at the caret — organize imports, generate the missing method, apply the suggested refactoring. Inspections are continuous static analysis; intentions are their actionable front-end. Ignoring them wastes the analysis; the workflow is: read the warning, Alt+Enter, accept or deliberately suppress.

scenarios.title: The sed rename
scenarios.situation: A developer renames a widely-used class with sed — catching the class, the comments mentioning it, and a string literal that happened to match. The build passes; the runtime breaks on the corrupted string. (Companion to the existing scenario 'Renaming across forty files.')
evidence: Observed: A developer renames a widely-used class with sed — catching the class, the comments mentioning it, and a string literal that happened to match. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Rename semantically (2) Preview refactorings Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct IDE rename refactoring?
choices: A. sed is fine; the string was bad luck.

B. Shift+F6 (rename refactoring): the IDE renames the SYMBOL — declarations, references, imports — via semantic analysis, previewing every occurrence before applying; strings and comments are offered separately, never silently — the 40 files change correctly, the string literal survives.
C. Rename by hand in each file; the IDE can't be trusted.
D. Don't rename; names are permanent.
scenarios.hint: Hint: sed corrupted a string literal. What distinguishes the symbol from same-spelled text?
scenarios.why: Text rename (sed) cannot distinguish the symbol from the string that spells the same — it operates on characters, and the corrupted literal is the proof. The IDE's rename refactoring operates on semantics: it resolves the symbol through the language model (declarations, references, overrides, imports), previews the full occurrence list, and applies the change as one atomic refactoring — with strings/comments as explicit opt-in checkboxes, defaulting to safe. The preview is the trust mechanism: you see all 40 files' changes before committing to them. The sed rename was fast and wrong; the refactoring is fast and right.

scenarios.title: The grep archaeologist
scenarios.situation: A developer needs every try/except that swallows exceptions (bare 'except: pass') across 200 files — grep finds 400 matches, most innocent. Each must be read by hand. (Companion to the existing scenario 'Browsing instead of searching.')
evidence: Observed: A developer needs every try/except that swallows exceptions (bare 'except: pass') across 200 files — grep finds 400 matches, most innocent. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Search structurally (2) Replace with templates Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct structural-search technique?
choices: A. Better grep; the regex just needs work.

B. Structural Search and Replace (SSR): search by CODE STRUCTURE (try: $stmts$ except: pass) not text — the IDE matches the pattern semantically across all types and nesting; replace templates fix all 400 at once with preview — the 400 text matches become the 12 real ones.
C. Read all 400; diligence is the job.
D. Forbid bare excepts; the past is unfixable.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 400 text matches, 12 real swallows. What matches code shape instead of text?
scenarios.why: Text search cannot express 'the try block whose except swallows' — the pattern is structural (a try statement with an except clause containing only pass), and grep's 400 matches are the text-shape of many different structures. SSR searches the IDE's syntax tree: the template try:/except:/pass with placeholders ($stmts$) matches the structure regardless of formatting, nesting, or variable names — the 400 collapse to the 12 real swallows. The replace template then rewrites all 12 (log the exception, re-raise, or handle) with the same preview discipline as rename. This is grep's semantic successor: where text search finds strings, SSR finds code shapes.

scenarios.title: The print debugger in an IDE
scenarios.situation: A developer debugs in IntelliJ with print statements — restarting the app for each hypothesis. The IDE's debugger sits unused; they 'never learned it.' (Companion to the existing scenario 'Interrogating the running program.')
evidence: Observed: A developer debugs in IntelliJ with print statements — restarting the app for each hypothesis. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Debug with conditions (2) Evaluate in paused frames Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct IDE-debugger workflow?
choices: A. Prints are honest; the debugger hides things.

B. Interrogate the running program: conditional breakpoints (pause only when user.id == 42), Evaluate Expression (run code in the paused frame's context), watches (track expressions across steps), Drop Frame (re-enter the method) — hypotheses tested in seconds against the live program, no restarts.
C. The debugger is for juniors; seniors print.
D. Restart-driven debugging is fine; restarts are fast.
scenarios.hint: Hint: each hypothesis cost a restart. What tests hypotheses against the live program?
scenarios.why: Print debugging tests hypotheses at restart-speed: each question needs an edit, a rebuild, a rerun, and a log read. The IDE debugger tests them at thought-speed: the conditional breakpoint pauses exactly the failing case (user.id == 42 — no wading through 10,000 good requests), Evaluate Expression runs arbitrary code in the paused frame (what if this were null?), watches track the suspect expression as you step, and Drop Frame rewinds the current method to retry with different inputs. The print loop's restarts were the tax; the debugger's live interrogation is the refund. 'Never learned it' was the actual bug — the tool was there all along.

choices: F5 always starts without the debugger — that's its purpose
F5 starts debugging (debugger attached); Ctrl+F5 starts without debugging — pick based on whether you need breakpoints
Both do the same thing — the difference is historical
F5 is for web apps only; console apps need Ctrl+F5
evidence: # developer presses F5 to 'just run' and wonders why it's slow
scenarios.hint: One attaches the debugger (breakpoints work, slower); the other just runs. Which is which?
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference, and when do you use each?
scenarios.situation: A developer always presses F5 to run and complains it's slow.
scenarios.title: Always debugging
scenarios.why: F5 = Start Debugging (debugger attached: breakpoints, variable inspection, slower startup); Ctrl+F5 = Start Without Debugging (just runs). If you're not debugging, Ctrl+F5 skips the debugger overhead. The choice is intent: investigating → F5; smoke-testing a run → Ctrl+F5.

choices: Use Debug > Attach to Process, select the running process — the debugger attaches to the live process with its symbols
You can't debug a running process — restart it under F5
Attach to Process only works for web apps
Copy the PDBs to the desktop — the debugger finds them there
evidence: # service running in production-like staging; bug only reproduces there
scenarios.hint: The process is already running and you can't restart it. What debugger feature joins a live process?
scenarios.prompt: How do you debug the running service?
scenarios.situation: A bug reproduces only in the long-running staging service; restarting loses the state.
scenarios.title: Debugging the unrestartable
scenarios.why: Attach to Process connects the debugger to an already-running process — breakpoints hit in the live service, with call stacks and variable inspection. Requirements: matching symbols (PDBs) and appropriate permissions. Restart-under-F5 is the common case; attach is the tool for 'it only happens after three hours of uptime'.

choices: The Immediate Window only runs in Release builds
Open the Immediate Window (Debug > Windows > Immediate) during a debug session and evaluate expressions / call methods in the current context
Immediate Window is a text editor — it can't execute code
You must add a Watch for every expression — the Immediate Window is read-only
evidence: # paused at a breakpoint; want to test `order.ApplyDiscount(0.1)` without editing code
scenarios.hint: You're paused in the debugger with full context. What window lets you type and execute code right there?
scenarios.prompt: How do you try the expression live?
scenarios.situation: Paused at a breakpoint, the developer wants to test a method call against the live state.
scenarios.title: The live experiment
scenarios.why: The Immediate Window evaluates expressions and statements in the paused program's context — call methods, inspect objects, even assign variables to steer the session. It's the debugger's REPL: test hypotheses (does ApplyDiscount fix the total?) without editing, rebuilding, and rerunning. Watches observe; the Immediate Window experiments.

choices: Reference the DLL by copying it into bin/ — simplest
Use the NuGet Package Manager (or dotnet add package) to add the versioned package reference — restorable, versioned, transitive
NuGet is only for Microsoft packages — third-party needs manual DLLs
Edit the .csproj by hand to add a HintPath — the modern approach
scenarios.hint: Manual DLLs don't restore on a fresh clone. What mechanism versions, restores, and transitively resolves dependencies?
scenarios.prompt: How should the dependency be added?
scenarios.situation: A developer copies a DLL into the project to use a JSON library.
scenarios.title: The DLL in the repo
scenarios.why: NuGet package references (<PackageReference> in the SDK-style csproj) are versioned, restorable (dotnet restore fetches them on any machine), and transitive — the package's own dependencies resolve automatically. Committed DLLs rot (which version? where from?), don't restore, and hide transitive needs. The Package Manager UI or dotnet add package is the one correct path.

choices: Build the solution in the Release configuration — Debug builds can't be deployed
Build configurations (Debug/Release) control symbols, optimizations, and conditional compilation — develop in Debug, ship Release
Configurations are just names — they change nothing
Always ship Debug — it has more diagnostics
scenarios.hint: What differs between the two besides the name — optimizations? symbols? What should production get?
scenarios.prompt: What do the configurations control?
scenarios.situation: A developer ships the Debug build to staging 'because it has better error messages'.
scenarios.title: Debug in staging
scenarios.why: Debug/Release are build contracts: Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance. Shipping Debug to production-adjacent environments is slower and can behave differently (timing, inlining). The dropdown also drives conditional compilation (#if DEBUG) — diagnostics code that must never ship.

choices: The .sln file lists every source file — edit it to add the class
Add the existing file to the project (or ensure SDK-style globbing includes it) — the project file defines membership; the solution just groups projects
Source files are auto-discovered — no action ever needed
Create a new solution per file — solutions can't share projects
evidence: # added Helper.cs to the folder; it doesn't compile ('type not found')
scenarios.hint: The file exists on disk but the compiler doesn't see it. What declares 'these files belong to this project'?
scenarios.prompt: Why doesn't the new file compile?
scenarios.situation: A .cs file added to the folder isn't compiled.
scenarios.title: The file the compiler can't see
scenarios.why: The project file (.csproj) defines compilation membership; the solution (.sln) merely groups projects. SDK-style projects glob *.cs automatically (so this usually just works), but classic/legacy projects list files explicitly — a disk file isn't a project file until added. 'Type not found' for a file sitting right there is almost always a membership problem.

scenarios.title: The service that can't be restarted

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct attach-to-process workflow?
choices: A. Restart it anyway; the connections will recover.

B. Attach to Process: the debugger connects to the RUNNING service (Debug > Attach to Process, select the service, choose the code type) — breakpoints bind to the live process, symbols load from the matching PDBs, the repro investigated without a restart; detach when done, the service never stopped.

D. Reproduce locally; production debugging is forbidden.

Attach to Process solves it: the debugger injects into the live process, breakpoints bind (given matching symbols/PDBs), and the investigation proceeds against the actual failing state — no restart, no repro rebuild, no dropped connections. The symbol requirement is the gotcha: the PDBs must match the deployed binaries, or breakpoints won't bind (the 'no symbols loaded' warning is the debugger telling you). Detach leaves the process running — the investigation is non-destructive. The log-only stance (choice C) accepts blindness where the tool offers sight.

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct MSBuild-diagnostic workflow?
choices: A. Clean, rebuild, reboot; the ritual sometimes works.

B. Read the build like a program: MSBuild verbosity to Detailed/Diagnostic (the actual command lines), the .csproj/.vcxproj as the file list (is the file INCLUDED? what Condition gates it?), the Output window's real errors — the 'invisible' file is usually excluded, conditioned out, or shadowed; the build log names it.
C. Delete bin/obj harder; the folders are cursed.
D. The file is haunted; rename it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the file is on disk but not in the build. What defines 'in the build'?
scenarios.why: The compiler only sees what MSBuild tells it: the project file's Include list, filtered by Conditions (Debug-only files, platform-gated sources), assembled into the actual compiler command line. 'Can't see it' has a short suspect list: the file isn't in the project (exists on disk, not in the Include), a Condition excludes it (wrong configuration/platform), or a stale obj artifact shadows it. Diagnostic verbosity prints the real command lines — the file's absence from the csc/cl invocation is the evidence. The clean-rebuild ritual (choice A) sometimes works because it clears the stale shadow — but the log would have named the cause in the first place.

scenarios.title: The staging debug disaster

C. Never debug staging; reproduce locally or give up.
D. The Debug build is honest; the timing change is fine.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the Debug build hid the bug by changing timing. What build keeps timing AND enables debugging?
scenarios.why: Debug builds distort the investigated system: no optimization (different timing — the race hides), extra checks and logging (the disk fills, the behavior shifts), different memory patterns. The staging bug then either vanishes (the Heisenbug) or the investigation creates new incidents (the full disk). The RelWithDebInfo-style configuration is the instrumented-but-faithful build: optimizations on (timing production-like), PDBs generated (the debugger and dump analysis work), logging at production levels. You debug the system as it runs, not a distorted twin. The configuration is the discipline: staging gets its own build flavor, neither Debug nor Release.

choices: Start changing code immediately — action beats analysis

Read the entire codebase — understanding everything precedes any fix
Ask a teammate to fix it — fresh eyes are the method

scenarios.title: The unreproducible bug
scenarios.why: A reliable reproduction is the foundation: it turns 'sometimes' into a deterministic trigger, gives you a before/after oracle for the fix, and often reveals the cause while you minimize it. Code changes before reproduction are guesses. The workflow — reproduce, hypothesize, instrument, verify — is what separates debugging from flailing.

Add a Console.WriteLine and rerun — prints are the only way
Give up — intermittent bugs can't be debugged

Both inspect production-fidelity state with zero code changes. Print-debugging the loop means editing, rebuilding, and drowning in 10,000 lines — the debugger filters at the source.

choices: The bug is in the code you wrote most recently — always

scenarios.title: The bug that only happens on Tuesdays

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct repro-first workflow?
choices: A. Fix the most likely theory; the repro is a luxury.

B. Hunt the repro before the fix: capture the full context (inputs, state, timing, environment), shrink it (delta debugging — remove halves until it still fails), automate it (the repro as a script/test) — the fix is then verifiable, and the regression test is free.
C. Add defensive code for all three theories; coverage beats precision.
D. Unreproducible bugs fix themselves; wait.

The repro-first workflow: capture everything (the input that triggered it, the system state, the timing — the bug's habitat), shrink ruthlessly (delta debugging: halve the input/state until the minimal trigger remains — the 10,000-line log becomes the 3-line case), then automate (the repro becomes a script, then a regression test). scenarios.title: The three hundred suspects

evidence: Observed: A regression appeared sometime in the last 300 commits. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct suspect-halving technique?
choices: A. Read all 300; diligence finds it.

B. Bisect: git bisect (or manual halving) tests the midpoint — good/bad halves the range each step; 300 commits fall in ~8 tests; the culprit commit identified exactly, its diff reviewed — the week's reading becomes an hour of testing.
C. Blame the biggest commit; size correlates with guilt.
D. Revert all 300; the feature isn't worth it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 300 commits, read in order, a week's work. What halves the range per test?
scenarios.why: Linear commit-reading scales with the suspect count; bisection scales with its logarithm — each test halves the range, so 300 commits need ~8 good/bad judgments, not 300 readings. git bisect automates the bookkeeping: mark the current HEAD bad, an old tag good, and it checks out midpoints for you to test — the culprit commit emerges exactly, with its diff as the prime suspect. The technique needs a fast good/bad test (the repro script from the repro lesson — the workflows compose), and it works for any ordered range: commits, config changes, even data versions. The biggest-commit heuristic (choice C) is astrology; the bisect is measurement.

scenarios.title: The trace that scrolls past

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct stack-trace reading technique?
choices: A. Google the top line; someone has seen it.

B. Read the trace as a map: start at YOUR frames (the application code — 12 frames down), read downward to the origin (who called whom into the failure), note the exception type and the exact line — the trace names the guilty call chain; the framework frames are the road, your frames are the addresses.
C. The top frame is the bug; fix there.
D. Traces are noise; add more logging instead.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the bug was the developer's own code, 12 frames down. Where should the reading start?
scenarios.why: A stack trace is the failure's biography: each frame is a caller, ordered from the throw point (top) down through the call chain. The top frames are usually framework/library internals (the road); YOUR frames — the application code that called into the failure — are the addresses that matter, often buried mid-trace. Reading technique: find your frames first (the code you own), read the chain downward (who called whom into the failure), and note the exact line + exception type (the what and where). The Google-the-top-line habit (choice A) outsources the reading to strangers — the trace already names the guilty chain; the pasted answer fixes someone else's bug.

scenarios.why: tasks.json (or npm scripts, Make targets, justfile) captures the project's command vocabulary as named, runnable, versioned entries — bound to shortcuts, composable (test depends on build), and identical for everyone. Retyped-from-memory commands drift; README commands rot. The runnable definition is the documentation.

choices: Run npm scripts directly — npx is redundant

Install every tool globally — globals are the standard

scenarios.title: The global install habit
scenarios.why: npx resolves and runs the project's local node_modules/.bin binaries — the version the project pinned, not whatever's global. choices: The shell is just a command runner — no learning needed

Use only the up arrow — history search is advanced
Aliases are cheating — type everything in full

scenarios.hint: Ctrl+R searches history; !$ reuses the last argument. What do these have in common — they treat your past commands as data?
scenarios.prompt: What shell skills pay off daily?
scenarios.situation: A developer retypes long commands from scratch every time.
scenarios.title: Retyping history
scenarios.why: Shell fluency — Ctrl+R reverse history search, Ctrl+A/E line jumps, !$ last-arg reuse, aliases for the 120-char docker invocation — turns the terminal from a typewriter into a tool. The commands you ran are searchable data; aliases version in dotfiles. Five minutes learning readline bindings pays back daily for a career.

choices: Keep the dotfiles in a git repo (bare repo or symlink farm in $HOME) — shell, git, and editor configs versioned, restorable, and diffable
Configure by hand on each machine — dotfiles are personal trivia
Dotfiles can't be versioned — they contain secrets
One giant .bashrc with everything — organization is overkill

choices: Run the command and hope — output is output
Pipe through the right tool: grep for filtering, jq for JSON, less for paging, tee for capturing — compose small tools instead of scrolling
The terminal can't process output — copy it to an editor
Bigger monitors solve output overload

The Unix pipeline turns firehose output into answers. Scroll-and-squint doesn't scale past a screenful — filtering does.

scenarios.title: The alt-tab developer
scenarios.situation: A developer alt-tabs between the IDE and a terminal 200 times a day — running tests, checking git, tailing logs. Each switch costs seconds and the mental thread. (Companion to the existing scenario 'The alt-tab loop.')

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Integrate the terminal (2) Bind frequent tasks Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct integrated-terminal workflow?
choices: A. Alt-tab builds character; the switches are breaks.

B. The terminal lives in the IDE: integrated terminal panels (split: tests | server | git), the working directory follows the project, tasks run the commands (one keystroke, output in-panel) — the 200 switches become zero; the context never leaves the editor.
C. Two monitors; the terminal gets its own screen.
D. The IDE is for code; the terminal is separate by nature.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 200 switches a day, each dropping the thread. What keeps the terminal in the context?
scenarios.why: The alt-tab loop is a context tax: each switch drops the mental thread (where was I in this function?) for a mechanical errand (did the tests pass?). The integrated terminal keeps the errands in-context: split panels hold the long-runners (dev server, log tail), the working directory tracks the project, and IDE tasks bind the frequent commands (test, build, lint) to keystrokes with in-panel output and problem-matching. The second monitor (choice C) reduces the switch cost without removing it — the eyes still leave the code. The integration removes the loop: the terminal becomes a panel, the task becomes a keystroke, the thread never breaks.

scenarios.title: The full-command typist
scenarios.situation: A developer types 'git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20' forty times a day — 45 characters, perfectly, every time. The typo rate is non-zero; the time is measurable. (Companion to the existing scenario 'The commands everyone retypes.')
evidence: Observed: A developer types 'git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20' forty times a day — 45 characters, perfectly, every time. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct shell-customization practice?
choices: A. Typing builds muscle memory; the 45 characters are training.

B. Aliases and functions for the frequent: short memorable names (glog, gst), functions for the parameterized (a function that takes the branch name), all in the versioned dotfiles — the 45 characters become 4, the typos vanish, the set travels to every machine.
C. GUI git clients; the terminal is the problem.
D. History search is enough; aliases are clutter.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 45 characters, forty times a day, typed perfectly. What names the intent instead?
scenarios.why: The retyped command is a function that hasn't been named: the 45 characters are constant except the intent, so naming the intent (glog = the graph log) compresses the typing and eliminates the typo surface. Functions cover the parameterized (gco <branch> — the argument varies, the shape doesn't). The dotfiles versioning (the dotfiles domain's practice) makes the set durable and portable — the aliases are part of the environment, not the machine. History search (choice D) retrieves the past; aliases name the future — the frequent command deserves a name, not a recall.

scenarios.title: The 400-line scroller
scenarios.situation: A build prints 400 lines; the error is somewhere in the middle. The developer scrolls, finds it, clicks the file:line, and repeats — five times a day. (Companion to the existing scenario 'Scrolling through 400 lines.')
evidence: Observed: A build prints 400 lines; the error is somewhere in the middle. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Configure build tasks (2) Use problem matchers Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct build-task practice?
choices: A. Scrolling builds reading speed; the 400 lines are training.

B. IDE tasks with problem matchers: the build runs as a task (Ctrl+Shift+B), the matcher parses file:line:column from the output, errors land in the Problems panel as click-to-jump entries — the 400 lines become a navigable list; the scroll retires.
C. Shorter builds; the output is the problem.
D. grep the output; the panel is unnecessary.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the error's file:line is in the 400 lines. What makes it clickable?
scenarios.why: The 400-line scroll is unstructured output navigated by eye — the error's file:line is in the text, but the text isn't actionable. Problem matchers structure it: the task definition includes patterns (regexes for the compiler's error format), the IDE parses each output line, and matches become Problems-panel entries — file, line, column, message, severity — each a click-to-jump. The five-daily scrolls become five panel glances. Shorter builds (choice C) don't remove the need to navigate errors; grep (choice D) finds the text without the jump. The matcher turns output into navigation.

scenarios.title: The VS Code Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that VS Code is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in VS Code?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — VS Code issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — VS Code is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is VS Code supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? objectives: Apply systems anatomy to VS Code
evidence: All VS Code components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.
