domains.name: Neovim
domains.description: Modal editing, motions, Lua configuration, and native LSP — the terminal editor as a full IDE.

scenarios.title: The new hire stuck in Vim
scenarios.situation: A new hire opens a file in Neovim to fix a typo, types their correction, and watches the text explode into random commands — they were in normal mode, typing as if it were insert mode. Twenty minutes later they still cannot quit.
evidence: Observed: A new hire opens a file in Neovim to fix a typo, types their correction, and watches the text explode into random commands — they were in normal mode, typing as if it were insert mode. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain modal editing (2) Navigate the mode round-trip Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct mental model for modal editing?
choices: A. Neovim is broken; use the mouse and menus instead.

B. Separate modes for separate jobs: normal mode is a language for navigating and operating on text (daw, ci"), insert mode is for writing new text, visual mode selects, command mode runs ex commands — you spend most time in normal mode composing operations, dipping into insert only to type; :q! quits without saving.
C. Stay in insert mode always; use arrow keys like any editor.
D. Memorize every key; modes do not matter.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the typed text became commands. Which mode interprets keystrokes as commands?
scenarios.why: Modal editing's power is the separation: normal mode turns the keyboard into a text-manipulation language where every key is a verb or noun (d=delete, aw=a word, i"=inside quotes), so editing becomes composable commands instead of mouse-choreography. The new hire's explosion happened because insert-mode typing in normal mode executes as commands — the fix is the mode habit: navigate and edit in normal, press i/a/o to enter insert for actual typing, Esc to return. Staying in insert mode (choice C) surrenders the entire advantage — it reduces Neovim to a worse Notepad. The modes are the editor; everything else is configuration.

scenarios.title: The developer who edits character by character
scenarios.situation: A developer fixes a misnamed variable by arrow-keying to it, holding delete, retyping — 30 seconds per occurrence, 40 occurrences. A colleague does all 40 with two commands.
evidence: Observed: A developer fixes a misnamed variable by arrow-keying to it, holding delete, retyping — 30 seconds per occurrence, 40 occurrences. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use motions and text objects (2) Apply the dot-repeat workflow Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct motions-first editing technique?
choices: A. Faster arrow keys; the keyboard repeat rate is the bottleneck.

B. Compose operator + motion/text-object: * on the variable to jump between uses, ciw to change each occurrence in place, or :%s for the global rename — motions (w, b, }, /) move by meaning (words, paragraphs, matches), text objects (iw, i", ap) select semantic units, and operators (c, d, y) act on them.
C. Use the mouse to select; precision beats speed.
D. Record a macro for everything; motions are obsolete.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the colleague changed all 40 in two commands. What moves by word-meaning instead of characters?
scenarios.why: Motions move by meaning instead of characters: w jumps words, } jumps paragraphs, /pattern jumps to matches, * jumps to the next occurrence of the word under the cursor. Text objects select semantic units regardless of cursor position inside them: iw (inner word), i" (inside quotes), ap (a paragraph). Operators (c change, d delete, y yank) combine with either — ciw means 'change inner word' wherever the cursor sits in the word. The 40 occurrences fall to * (jump) + ciw (change) repeated with . (dot repeats the last change) — or one :%s. The arrow-key crawl (choice A) optimizes the wrong thing: the win is semantic movement, not faster character stepping.

scenarios.title: The config that only works on one laptop
scenarios.situation: A developer's Neovim is perfect — on their laptop. On a new machine, nothing works: the config is a 2000-line vimscript pile with hardcoded paths, plugin manager state, and no documentation. Rebuilding takes a weekend.
evidence: Observed: A developer's Neovim is perfect — on their laptop. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Structure init.lua modularly (2) Version Neovim config Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Neovim configuration practice?
choices: A. Rebuild by hand each time; configs are personal snowflakes.

B. init.lua as versioned, modular code: Lua config in ~/.config/nvim versioned in git, split into modules (options, keymaps, plugins, lsp), plugin manager declarative (lazy.nvim spec), no hardcoded machine paths — the new machine is git clone + open Neovim, plugins install themselves.
C. Copy the whole ~/.config directory on a USB stick; versioning is overkill.
D. Use defaults; configuration is a waste of time.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the rebuild took a weekend. What would make it take one git clone?
scenarios.why: Neovim's Lua-first configuration is code, so it gets code discipline: versioned in git (the dotfiles lesson's practice), modular (options.lua, keymaps.lua, plugins/, lsp/ — each concern isolated, each debuggable alone), and declarative plugins (lazy.nvim reads the plugin spec and installs/updates on first run — no committed plugin state, no hardcoded paths). The 2000-line pile failed on all three: unversioned (laptop-only), monolithic (undebuggable), stateful (paths baked in). Defaults (choice D) forfeit the editor's compounding value; the USB stick (choice C) is versioning without history. The goal: a fresh machine reaches your full setup with one clone.

scenarios.title: The Neovim with no go-to-definition
scenarios.situation: A developer uses Neovim but jumps to definition with grep — the editor has no idea what a symbol is. Rename means sed. They assume 'real' IDE features need a 'real' IDE.
evidence: Observed: A developer uses Neovim but jumps to definition with grep — the editor has no idea what a symbol is. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Configure native LSP (2) Navigate code semantically Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Neovim LSP setup?
choices: A. Accept grep; terminal editors cannot do IDE features.

B. Neovim's built-in LSP client + a language server per language: vim.lsp.config enables the server (pyright, rust-analyzer, ts_ls...), the editor then speaks LSP — go-to-definition (gd), hover (K), rename, find-references, diagnostics, and format-on-save, all native, no heavyweight plugin framework.
C. Install every LSP plugin; more is better.
D. LSP is only for VS Code; Neovim cannot use it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: grep finds text, not definitions. What protocol gives editors semantic understanding?
scenarios.why: LSP (Language Server Protocol) is the industry's answer to 'every editor reimplements intelligence per language': the language server (pyright for Python, rust-analyzer for Rust) does the semantic work, and any LSP-speaking editor — including Neovim's built-in client — renders it. The setup is small: install the server binary (a package manager line), enable it for the filetype in the lsp module, and the keymaps (gd, K, gr, <leader>rn) light up. Grep-navigation (choice A) is text search pretending to be semantics — it cannot distinguish the definition from a comment mentioning the name. The 'real IDE' assumption (choice D) expired when LSP became the shared protocol.

scenarios.title: The developer who memorized the tree
scenarios.situation: A developer navigates a 5,000-file repo by expanding the file tree by hand — src/.../.../... — 20 seconds to open a file they half-remember the name of. The tree is a map of a city they traverse on foot.
evidence: Observed: A developer navigates a 5,000-file repo by expanding the file tree by hand — src/.../.../... Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Navigate with fuzzy finding (2) Search content with live_grep Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct file-navigation technique?
choices: A. Memorize the tree; familiarity is speed.

B. Fuzzy finding: Telescope (or fzf) over files (find_files), symbols (lsp_document_symbols), buffers, and grep (live_grep) — type fragments of the name, the matcher ranks, Enter opens — the 20-second walk becomes 2 seconds of typing.
C. More terminal tabs with find commands; the shell is faster.
D. Split the repo; 5,000 files is too many.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the developer half-remembers the name. What finds files from fragments?
scenarios.why: Fuzzy finding inverts navigation: instead of walking the tree to the file, you name fragments of what you want and the matcher finds it — find_files for names, live_grep for content ('where is this string?'), lsp_document_symbols for 'the function in this file', buffers for the open set. The tree-walk scales with repo depth; fuzzy finding scales with how well you remember fragments — which is how humans actually remember files. The matcher ranking (recent + frequent first) means the working set surfaces instantly. Terminal find (choice C) is fuzzy finding without ranking or preview — the same idea, worse execution.

scenarios.title: The recorded macro, replayed 500 times
scenarios.situation: A developer records a macro to reformat log lines and replays it 500 times with 500@q — on line 300 the pattern breaks (a malformed line), and the macro keeps 'fixing' subsequent lines into garbage. Undo is one giant step; the file is wrecked.
evidence: Observed: A developer records a macro to reformat log lines and replays it 500 times with 500@q — on line 300 the pattern breaks (a malformed line), and the macro keeps 'fixing' subsequent lines into garbage. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use macros safely Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct macro discipline?
choices: A. Never use macros; they are dangerous.

B. Scope and verify: test the macro on 3-5 lines first, replay on a visual selection (:'<,'>normal @q) instead of a blind count, keep the macro simple (one line per replay), and check :undolevels / use granular undo — the 500-blind-replay is the failure, not the macro.
C. Bigger counts; 500 was too few.
D. Macros cannot fail; the file was already bad.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the macro worked until line 300. What bounded the replay instead of a blind count?
scenarios.why: Macros replay keystrokes blindly — the malformed line 300 broke the pattern's assumptions, and the blind 500-count replayed the breakage 200 more times. The discipline: verify on a few lines first (does the macro do the right thing on the normal case AND the edge case?), replay over an explicit range (visual-select the lines, :'<,'>normal @q — the macro runs once per selected line, stopping at the selection's end), and keep macros to one-line transforms (complex multi-line edits belong in :%s or a script). Granular undo (or undo-tree) makes the wreckage reversible — the single giant undo step was the force multiplier of the disaster.

domains.name: Git in the IDE
domains.description: Staging, diffing, conflict resolution, blame, and history — version control without leaving the editor.

scenarios.title: The commit-everything developer
scenarios.situation: A developer's commits are all named 'fixes' and contain 14 unrelated files — they click 'commit all' in the IDE without looking. Bisecting a regression means reading 200-line diffs of mixed concerns.
evidence: Observed: A developer's commits are all named 'fixes' and contain 14 unrelated files — they click 'commit all' in the IDE without looking. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Stage with intent (2) Write diff-derived messages Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct in-IDE staging workflow?
choices: A. Commit all is fine; history is write-only.

B. Stage with intent in the Source Control panel: review the diff per file (click to see changes), stage hunks or lines selectively (not whole files), write the commit message from the diff you just read — each commit becomes one logical change, bisectable and revertable.
C. Use the terminal for git; the IDE panel is a toy.
D. Bigger commits; fewer is better.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the regression hunt failed because commits mixed concerns. What separates them before committing?
scenarios.why: The Source Control panel's real power is the per-file diff review before staging: clicking a file shows exactly what changed, and staging operates at hunk or line granularity — the debug printout stays out of the commit while the fix goes in. The commit message is then written from evidence (the diff just reviewed), not from memory. 'Commit all' (choice A) merges unrelated changes into unbisectable lumps — the regression hunt through 200-line mixed diffs is the interest on that debt. The IDE panel is not a toy (choice C); it is the diff-review step made unavoidable — the terminal lets you skip looking, the panel puts the diff in your face.

scenarios.title: The conflict resolved by picking sides
scenarios.situation: A merge conflict appears; the developer picks 'Accept Incoming' for every hunk without reading — shipping the teammate's half of a two-part change while deleting their own. The build breaks; the teammate's work vanishes silently.
evidence: Observed: A merge conflict appears; the developer picks 'Accept Incoming' for every hunk without reading — shipping the teammate's half of a two-part change while deleting their own. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Resolve conflicts deliberately (2) Use the 3-way editor Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct conflict-resolution workflow?
choices: A. Always accept incoming; the teammate is probably right.

B. Read every conflict hunk in the merge editor: the 3-way view (incoming | result | current) shows both changes with their context, resolve each hunk deliberately (take one side, both, or hand-edit the combination), then run the tests before committing — the conflict is a semantic question, not a coin flip.
C. Avoid merges; rebase everything always.
D. Delete the conflicted file and re-checkout; conflicts are unfixable.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the build broke because half a change shipped. What does each conflict hunk actually ask?
scenarios.why: A conflict is the version-control system asking a question it cannot answer: two humans changed the same lines, and only a human knows the intended combination. The 3-way merge editor presents the question properly — incoming change, current change, and the result pane — and each hunk gets a deliberate answer: take incoming, take current, take both (order matters), or hand-edit the true merge. Blind 'accept incoming' (choice A) answered 12 semantic questions with one coin flip — the deleted half-change and broken build were the price. The tests after resolving are non-negotiable: the merge result is new code that never existed before, and it needs the same verification as any new code.

scenarios.title: The line nobody understands
scenarios.situation: A developer finds a bizarre 5-line workaround with no comment. They ask around; nobody remembers. They delete it as 'dead code' — and the payment flow breaks in production. The line had a reason; the reason was in the history.
evidence: Observed: A developer finds a bizarre 5-line workaround with no comment. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Read history with blame (2) Delete with understanding Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct history-reading workflow?
choices: A. Never delete anything; all code is load-bearing.

B. Interrogate the line before touching it: git blame (or inline annotations) shows the commit, the commit message explains the why, the commit's diff shows what else changed, and the linked issue/PR gives the full story — the workaround's reason is one blame-click away; delete only with understanding.
C. Ask in chat; someone always remembers.
D. Comments are the only documentation; history is noise.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the reason was temporal, not textual. Where does the past live?
scenarios.why: Every mysterious line was written by someone for a reason, and version control remembers what humans forget: blame annotates the line with its commit, the message (if well-written — the staging lesson's payoff) states the intent, the diff shows the change's full scope, and the PR/issue link holds the discussion. The payment-flow breakage was a history-reading failure, not a code-reading failure — the code was legible, its reason was temporal. Inline blame (the annotation in the editor gutter) makes this a glance, not an expedition: the commit hash sits beside the line, one click from the story. Chat archaeology (choice C) works until the author leaves; history works forever.

scenarios.title: The 12-commit 'wip' branch
scenarios.situation: A pull request contains 12 commits: 'wip', 'fix', 'actually fix', 'oops', 'wip2'... Reviewers must reconstruct the real change from the archaeology. The author says 'that's just how I work.'
evidence: Observed: A pull request contains 12 commits: 'wip', 'fix', 'actually fix', 'oops', 'wip2'... Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Rewrite local history (2) Force-push safely Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct branch-hygiene workflow with interactive rebase?
choices: A. Push the wips; reviewers can figure it out.

B. Interactive rebase before review: reorder, squash the fixups into their commits (fixup!), reword messages to describe intent — the branch becomes 3 logical commits, each bisectable and revertable; the wip history stays in the reflog/local, the shared history tells the story.
C. One giant commit per PR; history detail is noise.
D. Never rewrite history; the wips are sacred.
scenarios.hint: Hint: reviewers reconstruct the change from 12 wips. What turns the draft into a story?
scenarios.why: Local history is a draft; the shared branch is the published story — interactive rebase is the editing pass between them. Squash merges the 'oops' into the commit it fixes (fixup! even automates the pairing), reword turns 'wip2' into 'Handle null cart in checkout total', reorder groups related changes — the result is a branch where each commit is one logical, reviewable, bisectable unit. The wips are not lost: the reflog keeps the draft, and the sausage-making was never the point — reviewers review the story, not the keystrokes. One giant commit (choice C) overcorrects: it lumps the logical units the rebase was meant to separate. The rule: rewrite local branches freely, never rewrite shared history.

scenarios.title: The interrupted deep-work session
scenarios.situation: A developer is mid-refactor (12 dirty files) when a production incident lands. They commit the half-done work as 'temp', fix the incident, then spend an hour untangling the 'temp' commit from the real fix — twice this month.
evidence: Observed: A developer is mid-refactor (12 dirty files) when a production incident lands. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Switch contexts cleanly (2) Use stashes and worktrees Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct context-switching workflow?
choices: A. Commit 'temp' faster; the untangling is just discipline.

B. Separate the contexts without fake commits: git stash (named: 'refactor-cart-midway') parks the dirty work, or a git worktree gives the incident its own working directory on another branch — the refactor resumes with stash pop, the history never sees 'temp'.
C. One branch per developer; context switching is the problem.
D. Finish the refactor first; incidents can wait.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the 'temp' commit claimed to be a logical unit. What parks work WITHOUT claiming that?
scenarios.why: The 'temp' commit pollutes history because a commit claims 'this is a logical unit' — and a parked half-refactor is not. Stash is the parking lot: named stashes ('refactor-cart-midway') preserve the dirty state with its intent, pop restores it, and history stays clean. Worktrees are the parallel desks: a second working directory on the hotfix branch, no parking needed at all — the refactor's files sit untouched while the incident gets its own tree. The IDE surfaces both (stash panel, worktree-aware windows). The hour of untangling was the 'temp' commit's interest — paid twice monthly.

scenarios.title: The rewritten shared branch
scenarios.situation: Friday 5 PM: a developer force-pushes a rebased main to 'clean it up.' Three teammates' Friday commits vanish from the remote. Monday is archaeology: reflogs, backups, apologies.
evidence: Observed: Friday 5 PM: a developer force-pushes a rebased main to 'clean it up.' Three teammates' Friday commits vanish from the remote. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Protect shared history Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct rule?
choices: A. Force-push freely; history should be clean.

B. Never rewrite shared history: rebase and force-push only your own unpushed/review branches (with --force-with-lease); shared branches (main, release) move forward with merges/reverts — the rewrite that 'cleans' main deletes teammates' work.
C. Nobody push on Fridays; the day is the problem.
D. Rebase main weekly; the team will adapt.
scenarios.hint: Hint: whose commits vanished? What distinguishes their branch from yours?
scenarios.why: The force-push rewrote the branch pointer: the remote's main moved backward past the teammates' commits, orphaning them. The rule is about audience: your private review branch is yours to rewrite (with --force-with-lease as the guard); shared branches belong to everyone — they advance via merges and reverts, which ADD history instead of rewriting it. 'Cleaning' shared history is vandalism with good intentions: the commits were not dirty, they were teammates'.

domains.name: AI Coding Assistants
domains.description: Inline completions, chat-driven development, and verification — pairing with AI without surrendering judgment.

scenarios.title: The developer who types everything
scenarios.situation: A developer hand-types boilerplate the assistant would have completed — imports, getters, test scaffolding — while the assistant's ghost text sits ignored. They 'don't trust it,' so they pay the typing tax on every line.
evidence: Observed: A developer hand-types boilerplate the assistant would have completed — imports, getters, test scaffolding — while the assistant's ghost text sits ignored. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use inline completions (2) Render fast verdicts Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct inline-completion workflow?
choices: A. Disable completions; hand-typing builds character.

B. Tab-through with judgment: accept the ghost text when it matches intent (Tab), partial-accept word-by-word when close (word-level accept), dismiss and type when wrong — the assistant drafts the predictable, you decide the meaningful; the typing tax drops while judgment stays.
C. Accept everything; the assistant is usually right.
D. Completions are only for juniors; seniors type.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the ghost text was ignored on boilerplate. Where is the assistant MOST reliable?
scenarios.why: Inline completions are a typing-tax refund, not an oracle: the model predicts the statistically likely continuation (the import block, the getter, the for-loop scaffolding), and your job is the 200-millisecond verdict — accept, partial-accept, or dismiss. The distrust-everything stance (choice A) pays the full tax to avoid the occasional bad suggestion; the accept-everything stance (choice C) ships the assistant's confident mistakes. The skill is the verdict speed: Tab for the obvious, word-accept for the close, Esc for the wrong — judgment per suggestion, not per session. Boilerplate is where the assistant is most reliable and you are most bored: let it type.

scenarios.title: The developer who chats badly
scenarios.situation: A developer pastes 2000 lines into the chat and asks 'fix it.' The assistant rewrites the file confidently — introducing three new bugs. The developer pastes the errors back, gets another rewrite, and loops for an hour.
evidence: Observed: A developer pastes 2000 lines into the chat and asks 'fix it.' The assistant rewrites the file confidently — introducing three new bugs. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Ask focused questions (2) Scope chat context Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct chat-driven development technique?
choices: A. Bigger pastes; the assistant needs the whole repo.

B. Small, contextual asks: select the relevant code (the selection IS the context), ask one thing ('why does this throw on empty input?'), iterate on the answer — the chat is a colleague: give it the file open, the error text, and a focused question, not the repo and a vibe.
C. Never use chat; it invents bugs.
D. Ask for full rewrites; the assistant scales better than you.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the loop never converged. What makes an answer checkable?
scenarios.why: 'Fix it' with 2000 lines is the worst prompt in the catalog: no symptom, no expected behavior, no boundary — the assistant must guess the bug, the fix, and your intent, and it guesses confidently. The technique: scope the context (select the function, or @-reference the file — the selection is the context), state the symptom (the error text, the failing case), ask one focused question ('why does this throw on empty input?'). The answer is then checkable — you can verify the explanation against the code — and the iteration converges instead of looping. Full rewrites (choice D) maximize the surface for invented bugs; the chat is a diagnostician, not a contractor.

scenarios.title: The merged hallucination
scenarios.situation: A developer accepts an AI-generated database migration without reading it. The migration drops a column the model 'cleaned up' — production loses data. The PR had one reviewer: the same developer, who skimmed.
evidence: Observed: A developer accepts an AI-generated database migration without reading it. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Verify generated code (2) Review AI output rigorously Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct verification discipline for AI-generated code?
choices: A. Never accept AI code; the risk is unmanageable.

B. Verify like a senior reviewing a junior: read every line of generated code, run it (tests, migration dry-run), check the edges the model glosses (destructive ops, error paths, auth), and require the same review bar as human code — the generator's confidence is not evidence.
C. The assistant is usually right; skim and ship.
D. Only use AI for comments; code is too risky.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the migration was skimmed, not read. What review would have caught the DROP?
scenarios.why: AI-generated code is junior-developer code at senior speed: fluent, confident, and wrong in the ways juniors are wrong — the dropped column, the missing null check, the hardcoded secret. The discipline is the code-review discipline, applied without exception: read every generated line (the fluency is the trap — it reads correct), execute it (the migration dry-run would have shown the DROP), probe the edges (destructive operations, auth checks, error paths — where the model's training data is thinnest), and hold the same review bar (the PR needs a real reviewer, not the author's skim). The model's confidence is a language-model property, not a correctness property — it is equally confident about the dropped column and the correct one.

scenarios.title: The assistant that suggested the wrong framework
scenarios.situation: The assistant keeps suggesting React patterns in an Angular project — its completions fight the codebase. The developer blames the model; the model never saw the project.
evidence: Observed: The assistant keeps suggesting React patterns in an Angular project — its completions fight the codebase. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Manage AI context (2) Write conventions files Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct context-management practice?
choices: A. The model is bad at Angular; switch tools.

B. Feed the assistant the project: open the relevant files (open tabs are context), use @-references/workspace context for the codebase, keep a project conventions file (the patterns the assistant should follow) — the assistant answers from what it sees; show it the project.
C. Disable the assistant for this project; it cannot learn.
D. More prompt engineering per message; context is manual.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the assistant guessed React. What evidence of Angular had it seen?
scenarios.why: The assistant's context window is its world: with only the current file's prefix, it guesses the framework from the code's surface — and guesses React, the statistically dominant pattern. The fix is context management: open files are context (keep the module's siblings open), @-references pull in the specific files (the component, the service, the spec), and the conventions file (AGENTS.md-style: 'this project uses Angular signals, standalone components, strict typing') sets the persistent frame. The React suggestions were not a model failure — they were a context failure. The assistant is a brilliant colleague with amnesia: brief it every session, in every project, and its answers align.

scenarios.title: The untested AI feature
scenarios.situation: A team ships AI-written features with no AI-written tests — 'the assistant doesn't write good tests.' Coverage falls; the features only work on the demo path. The assistant writes the code but nobody asks it for the tests.
evidence: Observed: A team ships AI-written features with no AI-written tests — 'the assistant doesn't write good tests.' Coverage falls; the features only work on the demo path. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Generate meaningful tests (2) Verify test teeth Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct AI-assisted testing practice?
choices: A. The assistant can't test; humans write all tests.

B. Generate tests from the code AND the spec: ask for edge cases explicitly ('test the empty, null, and oversized inputs'), generate the docstrings/README from the final code, then review the tests as hard as the code — the assistant drafts the suite, you verify it actually asserts behavior (not just runs).
C. Skip tests for AI code; it was generated correctly.
D. Tests slow the AI workflow; ship and monitor.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the generated tests passed but asserted nothing. What makes a test meaningful?
scenarios.why: The 'assistant doesn't write good tests' belief is usually 'nobody asked well': the default 'write tests' prompt produces happy-path smoke (calls the function, asserts no-crash) — because the ask was vague. The practice: prompt for the edges explicitly (empty, null, oversized, concurrent, unauthorized — the test-design thinking, delegated), generate docs from the final code (docstrings, README section — the code's behavior described after it exists), and review the suite skeptically (does this test FAIL if the code is wrong? — the mutation question; many generated tests pass regardless). The assistant drafts at speed; the human verifies the assertions have teeth. Coverage of the demo path is not coverage.

scenarios.title: The package that doesn't exist
scenarios.situation: The assistant imports 'react-super-date-picker' and writes a full integration — the package doesn't exist. The developer npm-installs the typo'd name and gets a stranger's typosquat package. The hallucination became a supply-chain incident.
evidence: Observed: The assistant imports 'react-super-date-picker' and writes a full integration — the package doesn't exist. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Verify AI-suggested dependencies Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct defense?
choices: A. Never trust imports; write everything from scratch.

B. Verify every generated dependency: check the package exists (registry search), pin versions, prefer the known libraries you already use — and treat unknown package names as the hallucination signal they are; the install of an unverified name is the incident.
C. The assistant knows the ecosystem; install what it says.
D. Typosquats are rare; accept the risk.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the package name was plausible but invented. What check comes before npm install?
scenarios.why: Language models predict plausible package names — 'react-super-date-picker' sounds exactly like a real package, because the pattern is real and the name is invented. The defense is procedural: every generated import gets verified (does this package exist in the registry? is it the one I mean?), versions get pinned, and the team's known-library list is the default (the assistant suggests the exotic; the project uses the boring). The typosquat install was the hallucination weaponized — the package name was the payload. Verify before install, always.

domains.name: Profiling & Performance
domains.description: CPU and memory profilers, flame graphs, and benchmarking — finding hot paths in the IDE instead of guessing.

scenarios.title: The optimization that optimized nothing
scenarios.situation: A developer 'optimizes' a function that felt slow — 2% faster. The real bottleneck, a JSON parse in the request path, was never measured. Two weeks of tuning bought 2% on the wrong function.
evidence: Observed: A developer 'optimizes' a function that felt slow — 2% faster. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Profile CPU hot paths (2) Read self-time correctly Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct CPU-profiling workflow?
choices: A. Optimize what feels slow; experience guides.

B. Measure first, then cut: run the CPU profiler (sampling) on the real workload, read the hot path (the functions where time actually accumulates), optimize the top frame, re-profile — the profiler replaces feeling with data; the 2% guess becomes a 40% fix on the JSON parse.
C. Rewrite in a faster language; the stack is the bottleneck.
D. Add caching everywhere; caching fixes slowness.
scenarios.hint: Hint: two weeks bought 2% on the wrong function. What would have named the right one in minutes?
scenarios.why: Performance intuition is reliably wrong about where time goes — the 'felt slow' function is usually the visible one, not the expensive one. Sampling profilers answer empirically: they interrupt the running program thousands of times per second and record the call stack, so the hot path emerges as the frames that appear most often. The workflow: profile the REAL workload (not a micro-benchmark — the request path under load), read the top of the stack (self-time vs total-time: the function burning CPU vs the one merely calling it), optimize the top frame, and re-profile to confirm. The JSON parse was invisible to intuition and obvious to the profiler — that gap is why the discipline starts with measurement.

scenarios.title: The service that grows forever
scenarios.situation: A service's memory climbs 50MB/day, restarting weekly 'as maintenance.' The team suspects a leak but has no data — just the graph going up and to the right.
evidence: Observed: A service's memory climbs 50MB/day, restarting weekly 'as maintenance.' The team suspects a leak but has no data — just the graph going up and to the right. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diff heap snapshots (2) Trace retainers Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct memory-profiling workflow?
choices: A. Weekly restarts are fine; all services leak.

B. Take heap snapshots and diff them: snapshot at baseline, snapshot after load, diff the retained objects (what grew?), trace the retainers (what holds the growth?), fix the reference (the cache without eviction, the listener never removed) — the leak is a reference graph question, answered by the snapshot diff.
C. Add more RAM; memory is cheap.
D. The GC is broken; tune the flags.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the graph goes up and to the right. What shows WHICH objects are growing?
scenarios.why: Memory leaks in managed languages are reference leaks: something still points at the objects, so the collector cannot free them — the cache without eviction, the event listener never unsubscribed, the static collection that only grows. Heap snapshots make the invisible visible: snapshot, exercise the workload, snapshot again, and diff — the growth is a list of object types with counts and retained sizes. The retainer trace then answers 'who holds this?': the path from the GC root to the leaked objects names the culprit (the unbounded cache's map, the forgotten listener list). Weekly restarts (choice A) treat the symptom on a schedule; the snapshot diff treats the cause once. More RAM (choice C) just delays the restart.

scenarios.title: The profiler output nobody reads
scenarios.situation: The team has profiler data but reads it as a flat list of functions — the call relationships are invisible, and 'the slow part' is a guess between 40 equal-looking rows.
evidence: Observed: The team has profiler data but reads it as a flat list of functions — the call relationships are invisible, and 'the slow part' is a guess between 40 equal-looking rows. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Read flame graphs (2) Prioritize plateaus over spikes Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct flame-graph reading technique?
choices: A. Sort by total time; the top row is the answer.

B. Read the flame graph's geometry: the x-axis is the sample population (width = time share), the y-axis is stack depth (each layer a caller), the widest plateaus are the hot code — click a plateau to zoom, read its stack downward to the burners; the shape shows the hot path, not just the hot function.
C. Flame graphs are art; trust the flat list.
D. The reddest frame is the slowest; colors are data.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 40 equal rows hid one call chain. What visual shows the chain?
scenarios.why: The flame graph's geometry encodes what the flat list destroys: width is time (the widest boxes consumed the most samples), height is the call stack (each layer called the one above), so a wide plateau is a function burning CPU and the tower beneath it is the call path that got there. Reading it: find the widest plateaus (the hot code), click to zoom (the context fills the view), read downward (who called this burner?). The flat list's 40 equal rows hid that 30 of them were one call chain — the flame graph shows the chain as a tower. Colors (choice D) are usually arbitrary or by package — the data is in the geometry, not the palette.

scenarios.title: The benchmark that proved the wrong thing
scenarios.situation: A developer benchmarks two JSON parsers with a micro-benchmark on a tiny payload, in a hot loop, with no warmup — parser B 'wins' by 30%. In production on real payloads, B is slower. The benchmark measured the harness, not the parsers.
evidence: Observed: A developer benchmarks two JSON parsers with a micro-benchmark on a tiny payload, in a hot loop, with no warmup — parser B 'wins' by 30%. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Benchmark honestly (2) Report distributions Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct benchmarking discipline?
choices: A. Micro-benchmarks are truth; production is noisy.

B. Benchmark honestly: warm up the JIT (discard early iterations), use production-shaped inputs (real payload sizes and shapes), measure with statistics (multiple runs, report distributions not single numbers), and benchmark the real path (the parser inside the request handler, not the bare loop) — the benchmark must resemble the decision it informs.
C. Benchmarks are useless; just ship and watch.
D. The fastest micro-benchmark always wins in production.
scenarios.hint: Hint: B won the micro-benchmark and lost in production. What did the benchmark actually measure?
scenarios.why: Benchmarks lie in predictable ways: no warmup measures the interpreter/JIT ramp instead of steady state, tiny payloads measure constant overhead instead of scaling, hot loops measure branch-predictor friendliness instead of real call patterns, and single numbers hide variance. The discipline: warm up (JIT, caches — discard the ramp), production-shaped inputs (the real payload distribution), statistics (runs, medians, p95 — not one lucky number), and the real path (the parser in the handler, with the surrounding work — the 30% 'win' evaporated because the harness was the measured thing). The benchmark's job is to inform the production decision; resemblance to production is its validity.

scenarios.title: The async app that waits in line
scenarios.situation: A Node.js service handles 20 requests/second though the event loop is idle 70% of the time — a synchronous crypto call blocks each request for 40ms. The async code awaits politely around a blocking core.
evidence: Observed: A Node.js service handles 20 requests/second though the event loop is idle 70% of the time — a synchronous crypto call blocks each request for 40ms. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diagnose blocking calls (2) Keep the loop unblocked Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct async-performance diagnosis?
choices: A. More async/await; the code needs more keywords.

B. Find the blocking call in the async path: profile with async-aware tooling (the event-loop lag, the blocked stack), move the CPU-bound work off the loop (worker threads, child process, or native async), keep the loop for I/O — the 40ms sync crypto is the queue; the loop was never the bottleneck.
C. Cluster more processes; scale past the block.
D. Async is a lie; rewrite synchronously.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the loop is idle 70% but throughput is 20 rps. What stalls an idle loop?
scenarios.why: Async runtimes serialize on the event loop: one blocking call (sync crypto, sync fs, JSON.parse on a huge payload) stalls EVERY request behind it — the loop's 70% idle is the tell (idle loop + low throughput = something blocking the turns). The diagnosis: event-loop lag metrics (the loop's delay between turns), async-aware profiles (which stacks block the loop), then the fix — CPU-bound work leaves the loop (worker threads for crypto, streams for big parses), the loop keeps only I/O multiplexing. More processes (choice C) multiplies the blocked loops instead of unblocking one; more await keywords (choice A) cannot unblock synchronous code.

scenarios.title: The fast local, slow production mystery
scenarios.situation: Locally the endpoint answers in 80ms; in production it's 2.5 seconds. The team blames the network for a month — then discovers the production database is missing the index the local one has. The environments differed; the code didn't.
evidence: Observed: Locally the endpoint answers in 80ms; in production it's 2.5 seconds. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Diagnose environment gaps Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct environment-parity diagnosis?
choices: A. The network is always guilty; add retries.

B. Diff the environments, not the code: compare schema/indexes, config, data volume, and dependency versions between local and production — the 80ms vs 2.5s gap with identical code is an environment difference by elimination; the missing index is found by schema diff, not code review.
C. Optimize the code; 80ms local is also slow.
D. Production is just slower; accept the gap.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the code was identical. What else differs between local and production?
scenarios.why: Identical code with different performance is an environment problem by elimination — the month of network-blaming was a failure to apply the elimination. The diff checklist: database schema and indexes (the missing index — the classic), configuration (pool sizes, timeouts, feature flags), data volume and shape (production's 10M rows vs local's 1K), dependency versions and infrastructure (instance sizes, regions). The schema diff finds the missing index in minutes; the code review never could, because the code was innocent.

domains.name: Remote & Dev Containers
domains.description: SSH remote development, dev containers, and reproducible environments — the end of 'works on my machine.'

scenarios.title: The vim-over-SSH struggle
scenarios.situation: A developer SSHes into a server and edits with bare vim — no LSP, no debugger, no extensions. The production-adjacent debugging that needs the server's data happens in a 1990s editing experience.
evidence: Observed: A developer SSHes into a server and edits with bare vim — no LSP, no debugger, no extensions. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Develop over SSH (2) Configure SSH hosts Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remote-development setup?
choices: A. Copy files locally, edit, scp back; the server is just storage.

B. Remote-SSH in the IDE: the editor runs its UI locally while the language services, terminal, debugger, and extensions run ON the server — full IDE intelligence (LSP, debugging, extensions) against the server's files, data, and environment; the local machine is a thin client.
C. Develop locally and deploy to test; the server is for running.
D. X-forward the whole IDE; pixels over SSH are fine.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the debugging needs the server's data AND the IDE's debugger. What puts both in one place?
scenarios.why: Remote-SSH splits the IDE across the network boundary: the UI (rendering, keystrokes) stays local for responsiveness, while the backend — file access, language servers, debugger, terminal, extensions — runs on the remote host where the code, data, and dependencies live. The bare-vim struggle (choice A) and the scp shuffle both accept a false trade: either the environment or the tooling. Remote development keeps both — the server's 64GB dataset with the local's full LSP and debugger. X-forwarding (choice D) ships pixels instead of protocol — laggy where the split architecture is crisp. The mental model: the editor is a client; the project lives where it must.

scenarios.title: The three-day onboarding

D. Everyone uses the same laptop image; standardize hardware.

scenarios.why: The wiki-page onboarding is environment-as-folklore: version drift (the wiki says Node 18, the code needs 20), undocumented steps (the env var someone forgot to write down), and the 'don't touch it' fragility. devcontainer.json makes the environment code: the image pins the OS and toolchain, features add the database/tools, the extensions list installs the IDE setup, post-create commands run the seed/migrate — all versioned WITH the repo, so the environment evolves with the code it builds. scenarios.title: The logs-only remote debugger
scenarios.situation: A developer debugs a remote service with console.log and redeploys — each hypothesis costs a 10-minute deploy. The bug takes three days; the logs were the only instrument.
evidence: Observed: A developer debugs a remote service with console.log and redeploys — each hypothesis costs a 10-minute deploy. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remote-debugging setup?
choices: A. More logs; redeploys are just the cost.

B. Attach the IDE debugger to the remote process: the runtime starts with the debug agent (inspect flag, debug port), the IDE forwards the port over SSH, breakpoints hit in the local editor while code executes remotely — the 10-minute hypothesis cycle becomes a 10-second breakpoint.
C. Debug locally; remote bugs are local bugs.
D. The debugger can't cross networks; accept logs.
scenarios.hint: Hint: each hypothesis cost 10 minutes. What makes it cost 10 seconds?
scenarios.why: The log-and-redeploy loop is debugging at deploy-speed: each hypothesis needs a build, a push, and a wait — the three days were mostly waiting. Remote attach debugging collapses the cycle: the runtime's debug agent exposes the process (node --inspect, Python debugpy, JVM JDWP), SSH port-forwarding brings the debug port to the local IDE, and breakpoints set in the local editor pause the remote execution — variables, stacks, and stepping, all live. 'Remote bugs are local bugs' (choice C) is sometimes true and sometimes the month-long mistake — the production-only bug needs the production-shaped environment. The debugger crosses networks fine; the logs were a choice, not a constraint.

scenarios.title: The team of snowflakes
scenarios.situation: Five developers, five subtly different environments — different patch versions, different env vars, different extensions. 'Works on my machine' is the team's catchphrase; the CI is the only honest machine.
evidence: Observed: Five developers, five subtly different environments — different patch versions, different env vars, different extensions. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Standardize team environments (2) Converge local and CI Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct team-environment practice?
choices: A. The CI is the source of truth; local differences don't matter.

B. One definition, every machine: the dev container (or Nix/VM image) versioned in the repo is the team's backend — local differences become impossible by construction; CI uses the same definition — the catchphrase dies because the machines converge.
C. Stricter wiki; the team needs discipline.
D. Identical laptops for everyone; hardware solves it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: five developers, five environments. What makes divergence impossible instead of forbidden?
scenarios.why: Environment drift is a team tax: the bug that reproduces for one developer but not another, the 'it passed locally' that fails in CI, the onboarding that differs per mentor. The fix is structural, not disciplinary: the environment definition (devcontainer.json, pinned image, locked dependencies) is the single source — every developer's backend is built from it, and CI builds from the same file. Differences become impossible by construction rather than forbidden by policy. The wiki (choice C) asks five humans to stay synchronized; the container makes synchronization the default. CI-as-truth (choice A) leaves local development as the wild west where most hours are spent.

scenarios.title: The month-long feature branch
scenarios.situation: A developer's feature branch lives for a month on their laptop — unreviewable, untestable by others, lost when the laptop dies. The branch is a rumor until merge day.
evidence: Observed: A developer's feature branch lives for a month on their laptop — unreviewable, untestable by others, lost when the laptop dies. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Use ephemeral environments (2) Review running branches Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct ephemeral-environment workflow?
choices: A. Merge faster; long branches are the problem.

B. Cloud dev environments per branch/task: one click spins a fresh container from the repo's definition, the IDE (or browser) attaches, teammates can open the same environment to review the RUNNING feature — the branch becomes a URL, reviewable and testable before merge; nothing lives only on a laptop.
C. Screenshots for review; environments are heavy.
D. The laptop is fine; backups solve the loss.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the branch was a rumor for a month. What makes a branch reviewable before merge?
scenarios.why: The month-long local branch is invisible work: unreviewable (no running instance), untestable (QA can't reach it), fragile (the laptop is a single point of failure). Ephemeral cloud environments fix the visibility: each branch/task gets a fresh, disposable container built from the repo's definition — the reviewer opens the environment URL and clicks through the RUNNING feature, QA tests the actual behavior, and the laptop's death loses nothing (the work lives in the branch + the reproducible definition). Merge-faster (choice A) treats the symptom; the environment-per-branch treats the cause — work becomes reviewable the day it starts, not the day it merges.

scenarios.title: The container that wasn't
scenarios.situation: The team 'uses containers' — but developers mount their local toolchain into the container and skip the image build. The container is a costume over the same snowflake; the bug that 'only happens in CI' keeps happening.
evidence: Observed: The team 'uses containers' — but developers mount their local toolchain into the container and skip the image build. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Keep containers honest Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct container-hygiene rule?
choices: A. Containers are theater; accept the snowflakes.

B. The container is the computer: build the image from the repo definition, develop INSIDE it (no host toolchain mounts), CI runs the same image — the costume becomes the machine; 'only in CI' bugs die when CI and local are the same computer.
C. Thinner containers; the image is too big.
D. Mount more; the host is faster.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the local toolchain leaked into the container. Where should the toolchain live?
scenarios.why: The mounted-toolchain container keeps the snowflake: the local Node 21 leaks into the 'Node 20' container, and CI — building the real image — sees a different world. The rule: the image builds from the definition, development happens inside the built image (extensions and tools installed IN the container), and CI runs that same image. Then 'only in CI' is impossible — there is one computer, and everyone (plus CI) uses it. The costume becomes the machine.

domains.name: Dotfiles & Environment Setup
domains.description: Versioning configs, bootstrapping machines, and secret hygiene — your environment, reproducible.

scenarios.title: The perfect setup, lost to a dead drive
scenarios.situation: A developer's five-year-perfected shell, editor, and git config dies with an SSD. The rebuild is archaeology: half-remembered aliases, a lost prompt theme, keybindings that will never be quite right again.
evidence: Observed: A developer's five-year-perfected shell, editor, and git config dies with an SSD. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Version dotfiles (2) Write bootstrap scripts Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct dotfiles practice?
choices: A. Screenshot the configs; rebuild from the pictures.

B. The home directory as a repo: ~/.dotfiles (or bare-repo) versioning shell/editor/git/IDE configs, symlinked into place — every tweak committed with a message; the dead drive costs one clone and a bootstrap script, not five years.
C. Cloud sync the home folder; versioning is overkill.
D. Defaults are fine; customization is vanity.
scenarios.hint: Hint: five years of decisions died with the drive. What preserves decisions?
scenarios.why: Five years of config tweaks are five years of decisions — the alias that saves 10 seconds 50 times a day, the keybinding that prevents the wrist ache — and unversioned, they are one SSD failure from extinction. The dotfiles repo makes the environment durable: configs live in git (history shows WHY the alias exists — the commit message), symlinks put them in place (~/.zshrc -> ~/.dotfiles/zsh/zshrc), and the bootstrap script replays the setup (installs, links, sets defaults). Screenshots (choice A) preserve pixels, not semantics; cloud sync (choice C) syncs the files without the why. The dead drive becomes an anecdote instead of an amnesia.

scenarios.title: The new-laptop weekend
scenarios.situation: A new laptop means a lost weekend: app store logins, package installs, license keys, the seventeen manual steps — each remembered halfway through, each done slightly differently than last time.
evidence: Observed: A new laptop means a lost weekend: app store logins, package installs, license keys, the seventeen manual steps — each remembered halfway through, each done slightly differently than last time. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Automate machine setup (2) Write idempotent scripts Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct machine-bootstrap practice?
choices: A. Weekends are for setup; accept the ritual.

B. The bootstrap as code: one script (or provisioning tool) that installs packages (brew bundle / apt lists), links dotfiles, sets macOS/system defaults, installs IDE extensions from a list — idempotent (safe to re-run), tested on a fresh VM — the weekend becomes 30 unattended minutes.
C. Clone the old disk; the new machine inherits everything.
D. Manual setup builds familiarity; the weekend teaches.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the seventeen steps lived in memory. What makes them repeatable?
scenarios.why: The manual weekend is unrepeatable by definition: the seventeen steps live in memory, each run differs, and the result is another snowflake. The bootstrap script makes setup code: the package list (Brewfile, apt list — declarative), the dotfiles link step, the system defaults (the dock settings, the key repeat rate), the IDE extension list — all in the repo, all idempotent (re-running is safe; the script checks before acting). Tested on a fresh VM, it proves the claim; run on the new laptop, it delivers the 30-minute setup. Disk cloning (choice C) inherits the cruft along with the config — the fresh start is the point.

scenarios.title: The API key in the public repo
scenarios.situation: A developer commits their dotfiles — including the shell config with export AWS_SECRET_KEY=... — to a public GitHub repo. The key is scraped in 4 minutes; the $3,000 bill arrives Monday.
evidence: Observed: A developer commits their dotfiles — including the shell config with export AWS_SECRET_KEY=... Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Keep secrets out of repos (2) Wire secret managers Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct secrets-in-dotfiles practice?
choices: A. Private repo; the secrets are safe there.

B. Secrets never in the repo: configs reference secret MANAGERS (1Password CLI, pass, env files gitignored), the committed config uses placeholders/variables, the bootstrap wires the manager — the public repo holds the shape, the secrets live in the vault; the 4-minute scrape finds nothing.
C. Obfuscate the keys; base64 is enough.
D. Secrets in dotfiles are fine; scrapers are rare.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the key was scraped in 4 minutes. What should the repo have contained instead of the key?
scenarios.why: The committed secret is compromised the instant it is pushed — private repos leak (contractors, breaches, the repo flipped public), and scrapers watch public commits in real time (the 4 minutes). The practice: the dotfiles hold the SHAPE (export AWS_SECRET_KEY="$(op read ...)" — the variable referenced, the value fetched), the VALUES live in a secret manager (1Password CLI, Bitwarden, pass) or a gitignored .env, and the bootstrap wires them (the manager's CLI installed, the vault unlocked once). Base64 (choice C) is encoding, not encryption — the scraper decodes it too. The public repo becomes safe to share: the shape is useful, the secrets are absent.

scenarios.title: The symlink spaghetti
scenarios.situation: A developer hand-manages 40 symlinks — some point at deleted files, three zshrcs exist (which one is live?), and the bootstrap script is a list of ln -sf commands nobody trusts.
evidence: Observed: A developer hand-manages 40 symlinks — some point at deleted files, three zshrcs exist (which one is live?), and the bootstrap script is a list of ln -sf commands nobody trusts. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Manage symlinks with Stow (2) Organize dotfiles as packages Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct symlink-management practice?
choices: A. Fewer configs; the links are the problem.

B. GNU Stow (or a link manager): the dotfiles repo organized as packages (zsh/, nvim/, git/), stow creates the symlinks per package (stow zsh), unstow removes them cleanly — the 40 hand-links become package operations; the live config is always the stowed one.
C. Copy instead of link; symlinks are fragile.
D. One giant config file; packages are overhead.
scenarios.hint: Hint: three zshrcs, unknown which is live. What makes 'live' unambiguous?
scenarios.why: Hand-managed symlinks rot: the deleted target leaves a dangling link, the three zshrcs multiply because nobody knows which is live, the ln -sf list is write-only. Stow inverts the management: the repo is organized as packages mirroring the home layout (zsh/.zshrc, nvim/.config/nvim/...), and stow zsh creates exactly the links for that package — stow -D zsh removes them. The package is the unit: installing the shell config is one command, the live config is unambiguous (the stowed package), and the bootstrap script becomes stow invocations instead of 40 ln lines. Copying (choice C) forks the config — edits to the repo no longer affect the live file; the link is the point.

scenarios.title: The work laptop with the personal config
scenarios.situation: A developer's dotfiles assume the personal machine — the work laptop gets the personal git email on commits, the gaming aliases, the personal API keys. The first work commit carries the wrong identity; cleanup takes weeks.
evidence: Observed: A developer's dotfiles assume the personal machine — the work laptop gets the personal git email on commits, the gaming aliases, the personal API keys. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Layer machine overrides (2) Automate git identity Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct machine-specific override practice?
choices: A. Separate repos per machine; sharing is the problem.

B. Layered config: the shared base in the repo, machine-specific overrides in gitignored local files (sourced conditionally: [ -f ~/.zshrc.local ] && source it), per-directory git identity (includeIf gitdir) — the work laptop sources work.local, the identity follows the directory, the personal never leaks.
C. One config for all; consistency beats correctness.
D. Remember to set it per repo; vigilance scales.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the wrong identity shipped on the first work commit. What sets identity by directory, automatically?
scenarios.why: The single-config assumption breaks on the second machine: the git email, the API keys, the aliases differ by context (work vs personal), and the 'remember per repo' strategy (choice D) fails exactly once — on the first work commit. The layered practice: the repo holds the shared base (the 95% that's identical), gitignored .local files hold the per-machine delta (sourced if present — the base never knows the specifics), and git's includeIf sets identity by directory (~/work/* gets the work email automatically — no per-repo vigilance). The work laptop's commits carry the right identity from the first one; the personal config never touches the work machine's repos.

scenarios.title: The key committed three years ago
scenarios.situation: A developer rotates a leaked API key — but the OLD key is still in the dotfiles' git history, and the repo was forked twice. Rotation didn't remove the exposure; the history is the leak.
evidence: Observed: A developer rotates a leaked API key — but the OLD key is still in the dotfiles' git history, and the repo was forked twice. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Remediate leaked secrets Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
choices: A. Delete the repo; the history dies with it.

B. Treat the committed secret as compromised forever: rotate immediately, purge from history (filter-repo/BFG) AND consider it still exposed (forks, clones exist) — then prevent recurrence (pre-commit secret scanning, the manager pattern) — the history rewrite limits future exposure; it cannot un-expose the past.
C. The old key is expired; no action needed.
D. Rewrite history quietly; nobody will notice.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the repo was forked twice. What does that mean for 'removing' the key?
scenarios.why: A secret committed to git is compromised — period. Forks and clones preserve it beyond any history rewrite, so the ONLY remediation for the exposure is rotation (the old key dies everywhere). The history purge (git filter-repo/BFG) then removes it from YOUR repo's future clones — hygiene, not resurrection. And the recurrence prevention (pre-commit hooks scanning for secrets, the secret-manager pattern from the start) is the actual fix — the leak was a process failure, and processes get fixed. Quiet rewrites (choice D) without rotation leave the exposed key valid; deletion (choice A) doesn't touch the forks.

scenarios.title: The capstone nobody saw
scenarios.situation: The environment is built but undemoed: no recording, no writeup, no tour. The fluency is real and invisible — the interview never sees it.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Demo environments; Write the narrative. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct capstone packaging?
choices: A. The environment speaks for itself; users will notice.

B. The proof package: a recorded tour (navigate, multi-cursor edit, debug, profile — at speed), the design doc + writeup (choices, trade-offs, the timing numbers), the repos linked (dotfiles, devcontainer) — the stranger test: a reviewer grasps the environment in 15 minutes.
C. A long unedited screen recording; the length proves it.
D. Screenshots of the theme; the aesthetics prove it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the fluency is real and invisible. What makes it visible?
scenarios.why: The undemoed environment is the unproven one: the interviewer can't watch fluency that was never recorded, and the future-you can't reconstruct decisions that were never written. The proof package: the tour (the layers demonstrated at speed — navigation, editing, debugging, profiling — the watchable fluency), the writeup (the design doc plus the build notes: choices, trade-offs, the bootstrap timing, what you'd change — the narrative), the repos (dotfiles, devcontainer.json — the artifacts, linked). The stranger test is the bar: 15 minutes to grasp the environment. The theme screenshots (choice D) show the surface; the tour shows the hands.

lessons.title: VS Code — Core concepts
concepts: Command Palette: the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) is VS Code's universal command launcher: type a few letters of any command — menu items, extension actions, settings — and run it without touching the mouse.
Keyboard-first navigation compounds: the palette removes the need to memorize dozens of individual shortcuts.
Launch.json in .vscode/ defines debug configurations: type (debugger, e.g. node/python), request (launch vs attach), program (what to run), plus args, env, and preLaunchTask.
Multi-cursor: for cross-file renames, F2 (rename symbol) is the language-aware tool — multi-cursor is for the local, mechanical case.

example.walkthrough: VS Code settings layer: user settings (personal defaults) < workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json, committed). Committing the workspace file makes format-on-save, the formatter choice, and rulers consistent for every clone — the repo carries its own editor contract. Personal preferences stay in user settings; project requirements go in the workspace file.

pitfalls: Common trap: the team must use the same OS for settings to apply.
Common trap: multi-cursor doesn't exist in VS Code.
Common trap: emmet only works in .html files.
Common trap: edit keybindings.json to add every command manually.

lessons.title: IntelliJ / PyCharm — Core concepts
concepts: Refactoring: shift+F6 Rename is a language-aware refactoring: it updates declarations, references, and (optionally) related files while respecting scope — a comment mentioning the old name isn't touched, a shadowing local isn't renamed.
Rename: the IDE's refactoring engine exists precisely so renames are safe, previewable operations, not hope-driven edits.
Navigation: professional IDE fluency is largely navigation fluency.

Search Everywhere (double-Shift) finds classes, files, symbols, and IDE actions by name; Find in Path (Ctrl+Shift+F) searches file contents with regex and scope filters; Alt+F7 finds usages of the symbol at the caret.

Debugger: the debugger pauses at breakpoints and lets you inspect the full state: Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) runs arbitrary expressions in the current frame, Watches track values across steps, and conditional breakpoints stop only on the failing case.

lessons.title: Visual Studio — Core concepts
concepts: Debugging: F5 = Start Debugging (debugger attached: breakpoints, variable inspection, slower startup); Ctrl+F5 = Start Without Debugging (just runs).
F5 vs Ctrl+F5: if you're not debugging, Ctrl+F5 skips the debugger overhead.
Attach to Process connects the debugger to an already-running process — breakpoints hit in the live service, with call stacks and variable inspection.
Immediate Window: the Immediate Window evaluates expressions and statements in the paused program's context — call methods, inspect objects, even assign variables to steer the session.
Debug/Release are build contracts: Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance.

example.code: # Solution Configurations dropdown: Debug | Release
example.walkthrough: Debug/Release are build contracts: Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance. Shipping Debug to production-adjacent environments is slower and can behave differently (timing, inlining). The dropdown also drives conditional compilation (#if DEBUG) — diagnostics code that must never ship.

pitfalls: Common trap: open the Immediate Window (Debug > Windows > Immediate) during a debug session and evaluate expressions / call methods in the current context.
Common trap: the Immediate Window only runs in Release builds.
Common trap: build configurations (Debug/Release) control symbols, optimizations, and conditional compilation.
Common trap: attach to Process only works for web apps.

lessons.title: Debugging Workflows — Core concepts
concepts: Reproduction: a reliable reproduction is the foundation: it turns 'sometimes' into a deterministic trigger, gives you a before/after oracle for the fix, and often reveals the cause while you minimize it.
Conditional breakpoints (break when order.Id == 7431, or when total < 0) stop only on the failing case; logpoints ('logpoints'/'tracepoints') print values without stopping at all.
Bisection is binary search on history: git bisect checks the midpoint commit, marks good/bad, and halves the range — ~9 steps for 300 commits instead of 300.

example.code:
System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set...
   at Shop.Orders.ApplyDiscount(Order o) in Orders.cs:line 42
   at Shop.Cart.Checkout() in Cart.cs:line 17
example.walkthrough: Read traces top-down: exception type + message (what), then frames (where) — the first frame in your code is the prime suspect (Orders.cs:42 dereferences something null). Framework frames below/above are context. The trace is the program telling you exactly where it gave up; ignoring it to read from main() discards the best evidence you have.

pitfalls: Common trap: bisect: check the behavior at the midpoint of the suspect range (git bisect for regressions, or halve the input), discard the innocent half, repeat.
Common trap: explain it to a rubber duck (or a teammate, or write it up).
Common trap: set a breakpoint at the loop start and press F5 10,000 times.
Common trap: understanding everything precedes any fix.
