lessons.title: Extensions & Settings — Core concepts
concepts: EditorConfig: manual reconfiguration is slow and lossy; the project-level contract (.vscode/, .editorconfig) covers team needs, sync covers personal ones.
Team setup: extensions.json recommendations prompt every fresh clone to install the team's extension set in one click — the project's tooling becomes self-describing. Treat your setup as code.
Principle: it's the lowest common denominator that actually works.

example.walkthrough: extensions.json recommendations prompt every fresh clone to install the team's extension set in one click — the project's tooling becomes self-describing. Word-of-mouth onboarding is lossy; forced installs are heavy-handed. Recommendations hit the sweet spot: visible, one-click, and versioned with the code they serve.

pitfalls: Common trap: review what each extension sends (many offer opt-outs), keep useful crash/usage telemetry for tools you trust, and disable or remove extensions that over-collect.
Common trap: everyone discovers extensions by word of mouth.
Common trap: force-install extensions via group policy.
Common trap: formatting can't be shared across different editors.

lessons.title: Terminal & Tasks — Core concepts
concepts: Integrated terminal: the integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) runs in the project directory with the editor's environment, and — critically — file:line references in output become clickable links that jump to the exact location.

Tasks.json (or npm scripts, Make targets, justfile) captures the project's command vocabulary as named, runnable, versioned entries — bound to shortcuts, composable (test depends on build), and identical for everyone.
Npx resolves and runs the project's local node_modules/.bin binaries — the version the project pinned, not whatever's global.

Retyped-from-memory commands drift; README commands rot. The runnable definition is the documentation.

lessons.title: Developer Tooling - Core concepts
concepts: Editors (VS Code) are fast and extended via extensions; IDEs (JetBrains) bundle deep language understanding - indexing, safe refactoring, call hierarchies. Match the tool to the codebase size and language, not to habit.

Debuggers beat print statements for state you cannot see: breakpoints (including conditional ones), step over/into/out, watch expressions, and the call stack. Reproduce the bug first, then bisect with breakpoints.
Linters (ESLint, Pylint) catch bug patterns; formatters (Prettier, Black) end style debates. Run both in CI so the main branch is always clean and reviews discuss logic, not whitespace.

Git CLI is universal and scriptable - learn it first. GUI clients (GitHub Desktop, lazygit) shine at staging individual hunks and reviewing diffs; the concepts transfer because it is the same DAG underneath.
Dev containers and remote development (SSH, WSL) put the toolchain in version control. 'Works on my machine' dies when the machine is defined in a Dockerfile.
launch.json and tasks.json make F5 debugging and builds repeatable per project. Commit the portable parts; keep personal absolute paths out of shared config.

example.code:
code --install-extension esbenp.prettier-vscode
cat > .vscode/settings.json <<'EOF'
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode"
}
EOF
example.walkthrough: Install the formatter from the terminal so setup is scriptable, then pin format-on-save in workspace settings. Every contributor gets identical formatting without thinking about it - style becomes infrastructure, not discussion.

pitfalls: Common trap: debugging only with print statements - learn conditional breakpoints and watch expressions for intermittent bugs.
Common trap: committing .vscode/ with absolute personal paths - keep workspace settings portable or gitignore them.
Common trap: disabling a linter repo-wide to silence one noisy rule - use a per-line disable with an explanatory comment instead.
Common trap: resolving merge conflicts by picking one side for every hunk - read each hunk; conflicts often need a combination, then tests.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Ides Tooling move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of VS Code
concepts: VS Code is a multi-step process within VS Code: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect VS Code to the broader VS Code ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  VS Code begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to VS Code. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating VS Code as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
