lessons.title: Modal Editing: Think in Modes
concepts: Normal mode is the home mode: keys are composable editing commands (operators + motions), not text — daw, ci", dap are sentences.
Insert mode is for typing new text only: enter with i/a/o, leave with Esc — the round-trip is the core habit.
Visual mode selects text for a subsequent operation; command mode (:) runs ex commands like :w, :q, :%s.
Mode awareness is the skill: the status line shows the mode; confusion about the current mode causes nearly every beginner disaster.

example.code:
Normal mode:  daw        -> delete a word
              ci"        -> change inside quotes
              dap        -> delete a paragraph
Insert:    i (insert)  a (append)  o (open line below)
Escape back to normal.  :w saves, :q quits, :q! quits unsaved.
example.walkthrough: Read the normal-mode lines as verb+noun sentences: d (delete) + aw (a word); c (change) + i" (inside quotes). The insert entries are the only keys that type text — everything else in normal mode acts. The : commands are the escape hatch every beginner needs first: :q! ends the 'cannot quit' panic.

pitfalls: Living in insert mode — the Notepad trap; the editor's power is entirely in normal mode.
Mode confusion — typing prose in normal mode (command explosion) or navigating in insert mode (arrow-key crawl).
Ignoring the status line — the mode indicator prevents the disasters; glance at it until the habit forms.
Remapping Esc to nothing — keep a fast exit to normal mode; many remap Caps Lock to Esc/Control.
lessons.try_it: Open any file in Neovim; practice the loop: navigate in normal mode, i to insert a word, Esc back — 20 round-trips without touching the mouse.

lessons.title: Motions and Text Objects: Editing at the Speed of Thought
concepts: Motions move by meaning: w/b words, e end, }/{ paragraphs, / search, * word-under-cursor — navigation without arrow keys.
Text objects select semantic units: iw word, i" inside quotes, it inside tags, ap paragraph — position-independent selection.
Operators compose: c/d/y + motion/object = one editing sentence (ciw, dap, y})— the grammar of Vim.
. repeats the last change: the multiplier that turns one fixed occurrence into forty.

example.code:
*            " jump to next occurrence of word under cursor
ciw          " change inner word (cursor anywhere in it)
.            " repeat last change -> next occurrence, . again
:%s/old/new/g " or the global rename in one ex command
example.walkthrough: The sequence is the whole lesson: * finds the family, ciw fixes one member in place, . repeats the fix as you jump with n. The :%s alternative shows the ex-command path for the pure rename case. Both beat the 30-seconds-per-occurrence crawl by an order of magnitude — this is the motions payoff made concrete.

pitfalls: Arrow-key navigation — character stepping; motions move by meaning and win by 10x.
Visual-selecting before operating — v then d when daw does it in one grammar; learn the objects.
Forgetting . (dot) — repeating the full ciw each time instead of one keystroke per occurrence.
Macros for simple repeats — macros are for complex sequences; . and :%s cover the simple ones.
lessons.try_it: Take a file with a repeated identifier; fix all occurrences using only *, ciw, and . — no mouse, no arrow keys.

lessons.title: init.lua: Configuring Neovim as Code
concepts: init.lua is Lua code: modular (options/keymaps/plugins/lsp), versioned in git — configuration with software discipline.
Declarative plugin management (lazy.nvim): the spec declares plugins; the manager installs on first run — no committed state.
No machine-specific paths: portable config works on laptop, server, and container alike.
Incremental and documented: each module has a job; a comment explains the non-obvious — future-you debugs present-you's config.

example.code:
-- ~/.config/nvim/init.lua
require("options")   -- vim.opt settings
require("keymaps")   -- leader key, shortcuts
require("plugins")   -- lazy.nvim spec: lsp, telescope, treesitter
require("lsp")       -- language servers per filetype
-- New machine: git clone ~/.config/nvim && nvim  (plugins bootstrap)
example.walkthrough: The four requires are the module map — each file owns one concern, so a broken keymap never hides inside plugin config. The comment at the bottom is the whole point: the config's install story is one line because the plugin manager is declarative. This is the shape every maintainable Neovim config converges on.

pitfalls: The 2000-line single file — unversioned, undebuggable, unportable; modularize it.
Committing plugin state — the manager's job is installation; the repo holds the spec.
Hardcoded paths — /Users/name/... breaks on every other machine; portable or it is not done.
Config without comments — the clever mapping unexplained; document the non-obvious.
lessons.try_it: Split any existing vim config (or start fresh) into init.lua + options/keymaps modules; version it in a git repo.

lessons.title: Native LSP: IDE Intelligence Without Plugins
concepts: LSP splits the work: language servers (per language) provide semantics; Neovim's native client renders them — no plugin framework needed.
The feature set: gd definition, K hover docs, gr references, rename, diagnostics, code actions, format — the IDE checklist, native.
Setup is per-language and small: install server binary + enable in config — 5 lines per language, not a project.
Diagnostics as you type: the compiler's voice in the editor — errors surface at the line, not at build time.

example.code:
-- lsp.lua: enable servers per filetype
vim.lsp.enable({ "pyright", "rust_analyzer", "ts_ls" })
-- keymaps (in keymaps.lua):
-- gd: go to definition | K: hover | gr: references | <leader>rn: rename
-- <leader>ca: code action | [d / ]d: prev/next diagnostic
example.walkthrough: vim.lsp.enable is the whole setup call — the servers are named, Neovim handles the protocol. The keymap list is the daily driver set: definition, docs, references, rename, actions, diagnostics — the six motions of semantic navigation. With these, the grep workflow retires the same day.

pitfalls: Grep-as-navigation — text search for semantic questions; LSP answers what grep cannot.
Plugin-framework LSP — the heavyweight distributions; the native client covers the daily needs with less.
No diagnostics keymaps — errors visible but unnavigable; [d/]d makes them a workflow.
One server for all languages — each language needs its own server; there is no universal binary.
lessons.try_it: Install one language server for your main language; enable it and use gd/K/gr for a full work session.

lessons.title: Fuzzy Finding: Telescope and the File Universe
concepts: find_files: fuzzy-match file names from fragments — the 20-second tree walk becomes 2 seconds of typing.
live_grep: content search across the repo with preview — 'where is this string' answered instantly.
lsp_document_symbols: jump to functions/classes in the current file — the file's own map.
Buffers + recent: the working set is one keystroke away — the editor learns your orbit.

example.code:
<leader>ff  -> Telescope find_files      " files by name fragment
<leader>fg  -> Telescope live_grep        " content across repo
<leader>fb  -> Telescope buffers          " open buffers
<leader>fs  -> lsp_document_symbols       " symbols in this file
example.walkthrough: The four pickers cover the navigation questions: 'which file' (ff), 'where is this text' (fg), 'where was I' (fb), 'which function here' (fs). The leader-key prefix groups them as one family — one mnemonic space for all finding. This is the navigation layer that makes the tree a fallback instead of a lifestyle.

pitfalls: Tree-walking large repos — the 20-second walk; fuzzy finding is the upgrade.
Memorized paths — brittle to refactors; fragments survive renames.
Grep without preview — the match list without context; the preview pane shows the neighborhood.
No buffer picker — re-finding open files; the working set deserves one keystroke.
lessons.try_it: Bind the four pickers; for one day, forbid yourself the file tree — open everything via fuzzy finding.

lessons.title: The Source Control Panel: Staging with Intent
concepts: Diff-first staging: review each file's changes in the panel before staging — the commit is assembled from evidence.
Hunk/line staging: stage the fix, leave the debug prints — surgical commits, not file-level lumps.
Messages from the diff: the summary writes itself when you just read what changed — 'fixes' is the message of the unreviewed.
One logical change per commit: bisectable, revertable, reviewable — the unit of version control.

example.code:
VS Code Source Control workflow:
1. Click a changed file -> diff view (your change vs HEAD)
2. Stage hunk: right-click a hunk -> 'Stage Selected Ranges'
   (leave the console.log unstaged)
3. Message from the diff: 'Fix null guard in checkout total'
4. Commit. Repeat per logical change.
example.walkthrough: Each step enforces the discipline: the diff view makes review unavoidable, hunk staging makes the commit surgical, the message-from-diff makes 'fixes' impossible. The console.log left unstaged is the whole lesson in one image — the panel lets you commit the fix without the scaffolding.

pitfalls: Commit-all habit — the 14-file 'fixes'; bisectability destroyed at commit time.
Staging whole files — the debug prints ride along; hunk staging is the scalpel.
Messages from memory — 'fixes', 'update'; the diff you just read writes the message.
Terminal-only purism — the panel's diff-first flow; use the tool that makes review unavoidable.
lessons.try_it: Make your next 5 commits via the Source Control panel: diff each file, stage hunks selectively, message from the diff.

lessons.title: Merge Conflicts: Resolving in the Editor
concepts: 3-way merge editor: incoming | result | current — both changes with context; the question presented properly.
Per-hunk deliberate resolution: take one side, both, or hand-edit — the semantic answer, not a global coin flip.
Tests after resolving: the merge result is new code — verify it like new code.
Understanding over speed: the conflict is a conversation between two changes; read both sides before ruling.

example.code:
Merge editor layout:
  INCOMING (theirs)  |  CURRENT (ours)
  ----------------------------------------
  RESULT (what will commit) <- edit here
Per hunk: [Accept Incoming] [Accept Current] [Accept Both] or type
the real merge. Then: run tests, then commit the resolution.
example.walkthrough: The layout is the workflow: both sides visible with context, the result pane as the workspace, per-hunk buttons for the easy cases and free editing for the real merges. 'Accept Both' with attention to ordering covers the independent-changes case; hand-editing covers the intertwined case. The test run at the end treats the resolution as the new code it is.

pitfalls: Blind accept-incoming — the coin flip; the teammate's half-change deleted silently.
Resolving without reading context — the hunk's surroundings carry the semantics; read them.
Skipping tests after merge — the untested combination; the merge result is new code.
Fear-driven file deletion — checkout-and-redo destroys both sides' work; the editor exists to preserve it.
lessons.try_it: Take a practice repo; create a conflict and resolve it hunk-by-hunk in the merge editor, then run the tests.

lessons.title: Blame and History: Reading the Past
concepts: Blame before deleting: the commit, message, diff, and linked issue — the line's biography in one click.
Inline annotations: the gutter shows who/when per line — the glance that prevents the archaeology.
History view per file: the file's timeline — refactors, fixes, and their order tell the design's story.
Delete with understanding: the workaround's reason found first; removal as a verified decision, not a guess.

example.code:
In-editor history workflow:
1. Hover/click the gutter annotation -> commit hash + author + date
2. Open the commit -> message explains WHY
3. View the commit diff -> what else changed with it
4. Follow the PR/issue link -> the full discussion
Then decide: keep, refactor, or remove — with the reason known.
example.walkthrough: The four steps are the line's biography: who, why, what-else, and the discussion. Step 2 is why commit messages matter — the staging lesson's diff-derived messages pay off here, months later, for a stranger. The decision at the end is the point: removal becomes safe when the reason is known.

pitfalls: Deleting the mysterious — the payment-flow lesson; blame first, delete second.
Chat-only archaeology — the author left; the history did not.
Reading code without history — the temporal reason invisible in the text.
Ignoring inline blame — the gutter annotation unused; the glance that prevents disasters.
lessons.try_it: Find three uncommented tricky lines in your codebase; write down each one's story from blame — then decide their fate.

lessons.title: Interactive Rebase: Rewriting History Safely
concepts: Interactive rebase as editing: squash, fixup, reword, reorder — the draft becomes 3 logical commits.
fixup! autosquash: mark corrections as fixups during work; the rebase files them automatically.
Local vs shared: rewrite your branch freely; never rewrite pushed-shared history — the force-push boundary.
Messages describe intent: 'Handle null cart' not 'wip2' — the story the next reader needs.

example.code:
git rebase -i HEAD~12     # the editing room opens
# pick  -> keep    |  squash/fixup -> meld into previous
# reword -> fix the message  |  reorder lines to group logic
# Result: 3 logical commits. Then: git push --force-with-lease
# (--force-with-lease: the safe force-push; aborts if remote moved)
example.walkthrough: The -i session is the editing room: each line is a commit, each command a revision. fixup lines (from fixup! commits during work) auto-arrange with --autosquash — the workflow rewards marking corrections as you go. --force-with-lease is the safety on the rewrite: it refuses to clobber teammates' pushes, unlike bare --force.

pitfalls: Pushing wip archaeology — the 12-commit review; the editing pass is the author's job.
Bare --force — clobbers teammates' work; --force-with-lease or nothing.
Rewriting shared branches — the published history rewritten under readers; local-only rewrites.
Squashing everything to one — the logical units lost; squash to stories, not to a lump.
lessons.try_it: Take a wip-heavy branch; interactive-rebase it into logical commits with real messages (on a copy first).

lessons.title: Stash, Worktrees, and Context Switching
concepts: Named stashes: park dirty work with its intent ('refactor-cart-midway') — pop to resume, history untouched.
Worktrees: parallel working directories per branch — the incident gets its own tree, no parking at all.
Stash panel in the IDE: the parked contexts visible and restorable — the parking lot with labels.
No fake commits: commits claim logical units; parked work is not one — the history stays honest.

example.code:
git stash push -m "refactor-cart-midway"  # park it, named
# ... fix the incident on a clean tree ...
git stash pop                            # resume exactly where you left off
# -- or --
git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix/branch  # parallel desk, no parking needed
example.walkthrough: The stash commands are the interrupt protocol: push with a name (the intent preserved), pop to resume (the state restored). The worktree alternative skips parking entirely — a second directory where the hotfix branch lives, both trees open in separate IDE windows. Either way, 'temp' commits vanish from the workflow.

pitfalls: 'temp' commits — the history pollution; the untangling hour, twice monthly.
Unnamed stashes — stash@{0} mystery meat; the name is the intent.
Stash-and-forget — the parked work fossilizes; pop promptly, or the lot fills.
Single-tree purism — the parallel desk refused; worktrees exist for exactly this.
lessons.try_it: Practice the interrupt: dirty tree -> named stash -> clean fix -> pop — then try the worktree variant.

lessons.title: Inline Completions: The Tab-Through Workflow
concepts: Tab/partial-accept/dismiss: the three verdicts — full accept, word-by-word, or reject; judgment per suggestion.
Boilerplate is the sweet spot: imports, scaffolding, getters — predictable text, reliable completions, maximum tax saved.
200ms verdicts: read the ghost text as you type — the skill is fast acceptance, not blind acceptance.
Dismiss freely: wrong suggestions cost one keystroke to reject; the fear of bad completions is overpriced.

example.code:
The loop: type the intent (def calculate_total():) -> ghost text appears
-> Tab (accept) | Ctrl+Right (word-accept) | Esc (dismiss).
Boilerplate: accept aggressively. Novel logic: read every token.
The rule: the more predictable the text, the faster the Tab.
example.walkthrough: The loop's three exits are the workflow: full, partial, reject. The boilerplate-vs-logic rule calibrates trust: predictable text gets fast Tabs, novel logic gets slow reads. This is the pairing contract — the assistant proposes at typing speed, you dispose at judgment speed.

pitfalls: Ignoring ghost text — the full typing tax; distrust priced per keystroke.
Accept-all — the confident mistakes shipped; the verdict is the job.
No partial accept — all-or-nothing on close suggestions; word-accept salvages the near-misses.
Trust as a session setting — 'I trust it' or 'I don't'; the verdict is per-suggestion.
lessons.try_it: For one hour, use only the three verdicts on every suggestion — count your Tabs vs dismissals and where each was right.

lessons.title: Chat-Driven Development: Asking Well
concepts: Scoped context: the selection or @-reference — the relevant code, not the repo.
Symptom + one question: the error text and the focused ask — checkable answers, converging iterations.
The chat as colleague: brief it like a human — what's open, what's wrong, what's asked.
Iterate, don't rewrite: diagnose first, then fix surgically — the rewrite is where invented bugs breed.

example.code:
Bad:  [paste 2000 lines] 'fix it.'
Good: [select 40-line function] 'This throws TypeError on empty
      input. The traceback: ... What's the minimal fix?'
The good ask: scoped context, stated symptom, one question.
Verify the answer against the code before applying.
example.walkthrough: The contrast is the lesson: the bad ask gives the assistant nothing to be right about; the good ask gives it everything — the code, the symptom, the question. 'Minimal fix' bounds the blast radius: the assistant answers the question instead of redesigning the module. The verification line is the pairing contract again: the assistant proposes, you dispose.

pitfalls: Vibe-based pastes — 'fix it' on 2000 lines; the unanswerable ask.
Full-file rewrites — the invented-bug surface; diagnose, then fix surgically.
No symptom given — the assistant guesses the bug; state the error.
Applying without reading — the chat's answer merged blind; verify first.
lessons.try_it: Take one real bug; ask it the bad way, then the good way — compare the answers' checkability.

lessons.title: Verifying AI-Generated Code
concepts: Read every generated line: fluency is not correctness — the confident tone is the trap.
Execute before merging: tests, dry-runs, REPL — the DROP shows itself when run.
Probe the edges: destructive ops, auth, error paths — where training data is thinnest, bugs cluster.
Same review bar: AI code gets real reviewers — the author's skim is not a review.

example.code:
# Verification checklist for generated code:
# [ ] Read every line (not skimmed)
# [ ] Ran it: tests pass, dry-run clean
# [ ] Destructive ops identified (DROP/DELETE/migration) - confirmed intended
# [ ] Error paths and auth checks present
# [ ] Second human reviewed
# The migration's DROP COLUMN fails line 3. Data saved.
example.walkthrough: The checklist is the review made explicit: each line is a failure class from real incidents. Line 3 (destructive ops) is the production-data saver — migrations and deletes get their own confirmation. The second human is the process backstop: the generator plus one skimmer is a single point of failure.

pitfalls: Skim-and-ship — the merged hallucination; fluency disguised as correctness.
Trusting generator confidence — the language-model property mistaken for evidence.
No dry-run on migrations — the DROP discovered in production; dry-runs exist for this.
Solo AI review — the author skimming their own accept; the second human is the bar.
lessons.try_it: Take one AI-generated snippet; run the full checklist on it — find what the skim would have missed.

lessons.title: Prompt Context: What the Assistant Sees
concepts: Open tabs are context: the working set briefs the assistant — keep the relevant files open.
@-references for precision: pull the exact files (component, service, spec) into the question.
Conventions file: the project's patterns written once (signals, standalone, strict) — the persistent brief.
Context failures look like model failures: wrong-framework suggestions are usually unseen-project symptoms.

example.code:
Project conventions file (conventions.md):
- Framework: Angular 19, standalone components, signals
- Style: strict TypeScript, no any, reactive forms
- Patterns: feature-folder layout, barrel exports
- Testing: vitest, one spec per service
The assistant reads this + open files + @-refs. React suggestions stop.
example.walkthrough: The conventions file is the briefing document: framework, style, patterns, testing — the four things the assistant otherwise guesses. Combined with open tabs (the working set) and @-refs (the specifics), the assistant's world becomes your project. The React suggestions stop because the evidence now outweighs the prior.

pitfalls: Blaming the model — the context failure misdiagnosed; the assistant never saw Angular.
Single-file context — the prefix-only world; the framework lives in the project, not the file.
No conventions file — the patterns re-explained per message; write them once.
Closed-tab working — the relevant files shut; the assistant briefs on scraps.
lessons.try_it: Write the conventions file for one of your projects; compare the assistant's suggestions before and after.

lessons.title: AI for Tests and Documentation
concepts: Prompt the edges: empty/null/oversized/unauthorized — the test-design thinking, explicitly delegated.
The mutation question: would this test fail if the code were wrong? — teeth, not just execution.
Docs from final code: docstrings and README after the code exists — the behavior described, not imagined.
Review tests as hard as code: the suite is a product too — skimmed tests are skimmed safety.

example.code:
# The ask that works:
# 'Write tests for checkout_total covering: empty cart, null user,
#  negative quantity, 10k items (perf), and concurrent checkouts.
#  Each test must fail if the implementation is wrong.'
# Then: run them, break the code deliberately, confirm they catch it.
example.walkthrough: The prompt names the edge classes — the assistant cannot guess your risk model, so state it. 'Must fail if wrong' is the teeth requirement, stated upfront. The break-the-code check is the verification: deliberately introduce the bug and watch the suite catch it — the generated tests earn trust by demonstration.

pitfalls: Vague test prompts — 'write tests' yields happy-path smoke; name the edges.
Toothless assertions — tests that pass regardless; the mutation question filters them.
No docs generation — the behavior undocumented; docs from final code are cheap.
Untested AI features — the demo-path-only code; the suite is the shipping requirement.
lessons.try_it: Generate edge-case tests for one function with the explicit prompt; break the code and verify the tests catch it.

lessons.title: CPU Profiling: Finding the Hot Path
concepts: Profile the real workload: sampling profiler on production-like load — the hot path under real conditions.
Read self-time vs total-time: the burner vs the caller — optimize the frame that consumes, not the one that delegates.
Optimize the top frame, then re-profile: the loop is measure-cut-measure — each cut verified by data.
Intuition is the enemy: the felt-slow function is rarely the hot one — the profiler overrules feeling.

example.code:
IDE profiler workflow:
1. Start CPU profiling, run the real workload (not a toy input)
2. Open the call tree: sort by Self Time
3. Top frame: JSON.parse in request handler — 38% of time
4. Fix: stream parse / cache schema-validated objects
5. Re-profile: 38% -> 9%. The 2% guess would never have found it.
example.walkthrough: The workflow's steps are the discipline: real workload (the measurement must represent production), self-time sorting (the burner's address), the top-frame fix (leverage), re-profile (verification). The JSON.parse line is the payoff made concrete — 38% of request time, invisible until measured. This is the shape of every successful optimization story.

pitfalls: Feeling-driven optimization — the 2% on the wrong function; the profiler names the right one.
Micro-benchmark profiling — the toy input; the hot path under load differs.
Total-time confusion — optimizing the caller instead of the burner; read self-time.
One-shot tuning — the cut unverified; re-profile to confirm the win.
lessons.try_it: Profile one real workload in your IDE's profiler; name the top self-time frame and what it costs.

lessons.title: Memory Profiling: Finding the Leak
concepts: Heap snapshot diffs: baseline vs after-load — the growth as a list of types, counts, retained sizes.
Retainer traces: the path from GC root to leaked objects — who holds the growth names the fix.
The usual suspects: unevicted caches, unremoved listeners, static growers — the reference-leak lineup.
Fix the reference, not the symptom: eviction policy, unsubscribe, bounded collections — the restart schedule retires.

example.code:
Memory workflow in the IDE:
1. Heap snapshot at idle (baseline)
2. Run the workload (the daily traffic pattern)
3. Heap snapshot again -> DIFF: +48MB in RequestContext[]
4. Retainers: held by ConnectionPool.listeners (never removed)
5. Fix: removeListener on connection close. Graph goes flat.
example.walkthrough: The diff names the what (+48MB of RequestContext), the retainers name the who (the listener list), the fix names the how (unsubscribe on close). Each step narrows: from 'memory grows' to the exact reference. The flat graph at the end is the verification — the leak fixed, not managed.

pitfalls: Restart-as-maintenance — the scheduled symptom treatment; the snapshot diff cures.
No baseline snapshot — the growth unmeasured; diff needs the before.
Blaming the GC — the collector frees the unreachable; the leak is reachable-by-mistake.
RAM as the fix — the bigger heap delays the restart; the references still grow.
lessons.try_it: Take two heap snapshots around a workload in your app; diff and name the top growing type.

lessons.title: Reading Flame Graphs
concepts: Width = time share: the widest plateaus are the hot code — the eye finds them instantly.
Height = stack depth: each layer called the one above — the tower is the call path.
Click to zoom: the plateau fills the view — context without the noise.
Read downward to the burners: the plateau's stack names the path — the fix location.

example.code:
Flame graph reading:
  wide plateau at 'parse'  -> 38% of samples (the hot code)
  tower below it        -> handler -> router -> server (the call path)
  click plateau         -> zoom: parse's callees fill the view
  narrow spikes         -> one-off costs, ignore (not the hot path)
Fix the plateau, not the spikes.
example.walkthrough: The annotated reading is the technique: plateau (what burns), tower (how it got there), zoom (the detail), spikes (the ignorable). 'Fix the plateau, not the spikes' is the prioritization rule the flat list could never give — the spikes are wide in the list and narrow in truth.

pitfalls: Flat-list reading — the 40 equal rows; the call relationships invisible.
Color-reading — the palette is not the data; geometry is.
Chasing spikes — the narrow one-offs; the plateaus are the leverage.
No zoom — the full graph overwhelms; the click isolates the hot region.
lessons.try_it: Open any flame graph (yours or a sample); identify the widest plateau and its call tower in writing.

lessons.title: Benchmarking: Measuring Without Lying to Yourself
concepts: Warm up: discard JIT/cache ramp — steady state is the truth, not the first iteration.
Production-shaped inputs: real sizes, real shapes — the tiny payload measured the wrong regime.
Statistics over anecdotes: runs, medians, distributions — one number is a rumor.
Benchmark the real path: the component in its context — the harness must not be the measured thing.

example.code:
import timeit, statistics
# Honest benchmark shape:
# 1. warmup: run 1000 iterations, discard
# 2. inputs: real payloads (sampled from production)
# 3. measure: 7 runs of 10k iterations -> median, stdev
# 4. report: 'A: 12.3ms (sd 0.4), B: 14.1ms (sd 0.5)' — not 'B wins!'
example.walkthrough: The shape is the discipline: warmup discarded, real inputs, repeated runs, distributional reporting. The report format ('A: 12.3ms (sd 0.4)') carries its own uncertainty — the single-number 'B wins by 30%' was the lie's vehicle. This is the measurement hygiene that keeps benchmarks honest.

pitfalls: No warmup — the JIT ramp measured as performance; discard the early iterations.
Toy inputs — the tiny payload; the scaling regime is what production exercises.
Single numbers — the lucky run reported; distributions or it didn't happen.
Bare-loop benchmarking — the harness measured; the real path is the question.
lessons.try_it: Re-run one benchmark you trust with warmup + real inputs + statistics; see if the winner survives.

lessons.title: Async Performance: Finding the Blocking Call
concepts: Idle loop + low throughput = blocking call: the signature — something synchronous in the async path.
Event-loop lag: the loop's turn delay — the metric that names the blockage.
CPU-bound work off the loop: workers, processes, native async — the loop is for I/O multiplexing.
Async-aware profiling: the blocked stack in an async context — the tool must understand the loop.

example.code:
Diagnosis:
  event loop lag: p99 45ms (should be <10ms) -> BLOCKED
  profile: crypto.pbkdf2Sync in request handler — 40ms/req
Fix: pbkdf2 (async) or worker thread; loop lag -> 3ms.
Throughput: 20 -> 400 rps. The keywords were never the issue.
example.walkthrough: The lag metric is the diagnosis in one number: 45ms of loop delay names the blockage before the profile confirms it. The fix moves the CPU work off the loop — the async variant or the worker — and the throughput jump (20→400) is the signature of an unblocked loop. The keywords were innocent; the synchronous call was the queue.

pitfalls: Await-sprinkling — more keywords around the blocking call; sync code doesn't await.
Process-scaling the block — N blocked loops; the fix unblocks one.
Ignoring loop lag — the metric unmonitored; the blockage invisible.
Sync-in-async blindness — the crypto call looked fine; the loop's perspective convicts it.
lessons.try_it: Measure your event-loop lag (or equivalent); find the largest blocking call in the hot path.

lessons.title: SSH Remote Development: The Server as Your Editor
concepts: Split architecture: UI local, language services remote — responsiveness plus environment fidelity.
Full intelligence remotely: LSP, debugger, extensions run where the code lives — the data never moves.
SSH as the transport: keys, config, multiplexing — the connection is infrastructure, set it up well.
Local as thin client: the laptop's specs stop mattering — the server is the computer.

example.code:
Setup: ~/.ssh/config -> Host prod-debug (hostname, user, key)
IDE: 'Connect to Host' -> prod-debug -> open /srv/app
Result: terminal IS the server, debugger attaches to server
processes, LSP indexes server files. The 1990s editing ends.
example.walkthrough: The ssh config entry is the foundation — named hosts, keys, multiplexing — used by every tool, not just the IDE. The 'Connect to Host' step is the whole UX: one action, and the editor's backend relocates. The result line is the payoff: every IDE capability, now against the real environment.

pitfalls: scp shuffle — the copy-edit-copy loop; the editor can live on the server.
Bare server vim — the 1990s experience accepted; the backend split is the upgrade.
X-forwarding — pixels over SSH; the protocol split is crisper.
Local-only development — the production-adjacent debugging exiled; develop where the data is.
lessons.try_it: Set up one SSH host in ~/.ssh/config; connect your IDE to it and run the debugger against a remote process.

lessons.title: Dev Containers: Dockerfile + devcontainer.json
concepts: devcontainer.json as code: image, features, extensions, ports, setup — the environment versioned with the repo.
Onboarding in minutes: open folder -> container builds -> code — the three days become five minutes.
Environment evolves with code: the Node 20 bump is a PR to devcontainer.json — reviewed, tested, rolled out.
Disposable and identical: everyone's backend is the same container — 'works on my machine' retired.

example.code:
{
  "name": "app-dev",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/javascript-node:20",
  "features": { "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/postgres:1": {} },
  "customizations": { "vscode": { "extensions": ["dbaeumer.vscode-eslint"] } },
  "postCreateCommand": "npm install && npm run db:migrate",
  "forwardPorts": [3000, 5432]
}
example.walkthrough: Each key is an onboarding step automated: the image (toolchain pinned), features (postgres without installing it), extensions (the IDE setup), postCreateCommand (the wiki's 'then run...' steps), forwardPorts (the app reachable). The new hire runs zero wiki steps — the container runs them. This is the environment-as-code payoff in one file.

pitfalls: Wiki onboarding — the 2022 page; the environment definition rots separately from the code.
Unversioned environments — the 'don't touch it' machine; the container is disposable by design.
Manual toolchain installs — the Node-version drift; the image pins it.
Skipping post-create — the seed/migrate forgotten; the setup commands are in the file.
lessons.try_it: Add a devcontainer.json to one project; onboard a colleague (or yourself, fresh clone) with it and time the setup.

lessons.title: Port Forwarding and Remote Debugging
concepts: Debug agent on the runtime: --inspect, debugpy, JDWP — the process exposes itself for debugging.
SSH port forwarding: the debug port tunneled to the local IDE — the network crossed securely.
Breakpoints in the local editor, execution remote: variables, stacks, stepping — the full debugger, remotely.
Hypothesis cycle collapsed: 10 minutes -> 10 seconds — the three-day bug becomes an afternoon.

example.code:
# Remote: node --inspect=0.0.0.0:9229 app.js   (debug agent on)
# SSH: ssh -L 9229:localhost:9229 prod-debug   (forward the port)
# IDE: 'Attach to Node Process' -> localhost:9229
# Set breakpoints in your editor. They hit. Inspect, step, fix.
example.walkthrough: The three lines are the whole setup: the runtime exposes the agent, SSH forwards the port, the IDE attaches. The breakpoints-then-hit line is the payoff — the local editor is now the remote process's debugger. Every runtime has its variant; the pattern (expose, forward, attach) is universal.

pitfalls: Log-and-redeploy — the 10-minute hypothesis; the debugger is the 10-second one.
No debug agent — the process unexposed; the flag is the first step.
Exposed debug ports — the agent on 0.0.0.0 without SSH tunneling; forward, don't expose.
Local-only debugging — the production-shaped bug exiled; attach where it lives.
lessons.try_it: Forward one debug port over SSH and attach your IDE to a remote (or container) process this week.

lessons.title: Reproducible Environments for Teams
concepts: Single environment definition: the repo's container config — every backend built from one source.
CI uses the same definition: local and CI converge — 'passed locally' means something again.
Pinned everything: image, dependencies, extensions — the drift has nowhere to hide.
Onboarding = the definition: the new hire inherits the team's environment, not a snowflake.

example.code:
Team environment contract:
- devcontainer.json in the repo (the definition)
- CI builds the same image (the proof)
- Dependency lockfiles committed (the pins)
- 'It works in the container' is the bar (not 'on my machine')
Result: the catchphrase retires; the CI stops being the only honest machine.
example.walkthrough: The contract's four lines are the convergence: one definition, CI proof, pinned deps, and the new bar. 'It works in the container' replaces 'on my machine' as the claim — and the claim is now verifiable by everyone, because everyone has the container.

pitfalls: Wiki discipline — the five humans asked to stay synced; the container syncs by construction.
CI-only truth — local stays wild; most hours are local.
Unpinned dependencies — the drift's hiding place; lockfiles committed.
Snowflake acceptance — the catchphrase normalized; the tax paid daily.
lessons.try_it: Audit your team's environment drift: list three differences between any two dev machines, then containerize one away.

lessons.title: Ephemeral Environments: Codespaces-Style Flows
concepts: Environment per branch: fresh container from the repo definition — the branch as a running URL.
Review the running feature: teammates click through behavior, not just diff — the review deepens.
Disposable by design: the environment dies, the branch and definition persist — nothing laptop-local.
Day-one visibility: work reviewable from the first push — the month of invisibility ends.

example.code:
Ephemeral flow:
1. Push branch -> environment spins from devcontainer.json (minutes)
2. Share the URL: reviewer opens the RUNNING feature in a browser IDE
3. QA tests against the environment's forwarded ports
4. Merge -> environment dies. The branch was never a rumor.
example.walkthrough: The flow's steps are the visibility: spin (from the definition — reproducibility), share (the URL — reviewability), test (forwarded ports — QA-ability), die (disposability — no residue). The branch's lifecycle now includes a running instance from day one — the merge-day surprise becomes impossible.

pitfalls: Local-only branches — the month of invisibility; the environment URL is the fix.
Screenshot reviews — the behavior undescribed; the running instance is the review.
Laptop-single-point — the dead laptop loses the month; the cloud environment persists.
Merge-day surprises — the unreviewable branch; day-one visibility prevents them.
lessons.try_it: Spin one ephemeral environment for a current branch; share it with a teammate for a live review.

lessons.title: Versioning Your Config with Git
concepts: Home as a repo: shell, editor, git, IDE configs versioned — the environment with history.
Symlinks into place: one source of truth, linked where tools expect — edit once, reflected everywhere.
Messages explain the why: 'alias g=git: 50x/day' — the tweak's reason, preserved.
Bootstrap script: clone + run = the machine reborn — the dead drive costs an hour, not five years.

example.code:
# The dotfiles shape:
~/.dotfiles/  (git repo)
  zsh/zshrc  -> ~/.zshrc
  nvim/      -> ~/.config/nvim
  git/gitconfig -> ~/.gitconfig
  bootstrap.sh  # symlinks everything, installs packages
# New machine: git clone <repo> ~/.dotfiles && ./bootstrap.sh
example.walkthrough: The tree is the practice: one repo, configs grouped by tool, symlinks as the deployment, bootstrap.sh as the installer. The clone-and-run line is the recovery story — the five-year setup resurrected in minutes. This is the foundation the Neovim-config lesson assumed: init.lua lives here too.

pitfalls: Unversioned home — the dead-drive amnesia; the repo is the backup with reasons.
Copy-paste configs — the forked zshrc on three machines; symlinks keep one truth.
No bootstrap — the setup documented in memory; the script replays it.
Screenshot backups — the pixels without semantics; git keeps both.
lessons.try_it: Start the repo today: move one config (zshrc or gitconfig) in, symlink it, commit with a why-message.

lessons.title: Bootstrapping a New Machine
concepts: Bootstrap as code: packages, links, defaults, extensions — the setup in the repo, not in memory.
Idempotent: safe to re-run — the script checks state before acting; reruns converge.
Declarative package lists: Brewfile/apt lists — the toolchain as data, installed in one command.
Tested on fresh VMs: the proof — the script earns trust before the new-laptop day.

example.code:
# bootstrap.sh (idempotent):
command -v brew >/dev/null || install_brew      # only if missing
brew bundle --file=Brewfile                        # declarative packages
./link-dotfiles.sh                                 # symlinks (skip existing)
code --install-extension < list.txt                 # IDE extensions
defaults write ...                                  # system defaults
# Re-run anytime: converges, never duplicates.
example.walkthrough: Each line guards itself: the brew check, the bundle's convergence, the symlink skip, the idempotent defaults. The re-run comment is the property that matters — the script is safe on a half-configured machine, so it doubles as the repair tool. The new-laptop weekend becomes: run script, get coffee, code.

pitfalls: Memory-based setup — the seventeen half-remembered steps; the script remembers all of them.
Non-idempotent scripts — the re-run duplicates; guard every action.
Disk cloning — the cruft inherited; the fresh start is the point.
Untested bootstrap — the script's first run is laptop day; prove it on a VM first.
lessons.try_it: Write the bootstrap for your current machine (package list + one idempotent step); test the step by re-running it.

lessons.title: Secrets in Dotfiles: What NOT to Commit
concepts: Shape, not values: configs reference the secret manager — the variable present, the value fetched at runtime.
Secret managers as the source: 1Password CLI / pass / Bitwarden — the vault, not the repo.
Gitignored .env for locals: the values' file never committed — the .gitignore is the guard.
Public-safe dotfiles: the repo shareable — nothing in it compromises anything if scraped.

example.code:
# WRONG (committed):  export AWS_SECRET_KEY="AKIA..."  # scraped in 4 min
# RIGHT (committed):
export AWS_SECRET_KEY="$(op read op://vault/aws/secret)"  # fetched live
# .env (gitignored): AWS_SECRET_KEY=...   # local override, never pushed
# The repo holds shapes; the vault holds secrets.
example.walkthrough: The wrong/right contrast is the whole lesson: the committed literal vs the runtime fetch. The op read pattern keeps the shell config functional — the variable resolves at shell startup from the vault — while the repo stays public-safe. The gitignored .env covers the cases the manager doesn't; the .gitignore is the backstop.

pitfalls: Committed secrets — the 4-minute scrape; the push is the compromise.
Private-repo complacency — the repo flipped, shared, or breached; the secret was in git either way.
Base64 'encryption' — the encoding decoded by the scraper; obfuscation is not security.
Secrets in shell history — the export typed live; the manager avoids the plaintext entirely.
lessons.try_it: Grep your dotfiles for secret patterns (KEY=, TOKEN=, SECRET=); move every hit to the manager or gitignored .env.

lessons.title: Stow and Symlinks: Managing the Links
concepts: Stow packages: repo organized as zsh/, nvim/, git/ — the package is the install unit.
stow/unstow: one command links, one removes — the 40 hand-links become package ops.
Live = stowed: the symlink target is the repo file — edit the repo, the live config changes.
Bootstrap as stow list: the script stows packages — readable, re-runnable, trustworthy.

example.code:
~/.dotfiles/          # stow packages mirror $HOME layout
  zsh/.zshrc
  nvim/.config/nvim/init.lua
  git/.gitconfig
$ stow zsh nvim git     # creates ~/.zshrc -> dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc ...
$ stow -D nvim          # cleanly unlink one package
example.walkthrough: The tree mirrors $HOME — stow's convention: package paths map onto the home directory. The stow command is the installer: one command per package, links created exactly. The -D is the uninstaller — the hand-managed spaghetti's missing feature: clean removal.

pitfalls: Hand-rolled ln lists — the write-only bootstrap; stow is the readable version.
Dangling links — the deleted targets; stow -D cleans per package.
Copied configs — the fork; the symlink keeps one truth.
Mystery live files — the three zshrcs; stowed packages are unambiguous.
lessons.try_it: Reorganize one config area as a stow package; stow it and verify the live file resolves to the repo.

lessons.title: Machine-Specific Overrides
concepts: Layered configs: shared base + gitignored .local overrides — the 95% shared, the 5% per-machine.
Conditional sourcing: [ -f ~/.zshrc.local ] && source — the base adapts without knowing specifics.
includeIf for git identity: gitdir:~/work/ -> work email — the identity follows the directory, automatically.
No leakage by construction: the personal never enters the work context — the layering guarantees it.

example.code:
# ~/.zshrc (shared, committed):
[ -f ~/.zshrc.local ] && source ~/.zshrc.local  # machine delta
# ~/.gitconfig (shared, committed):
[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
  path = ~/.gitconfig-work   # work email, signing key
# ~/.gitconfig-work: gitignored... or committed? committed is fine (no secrets)
example.walkthrough: The conditional source is the layering mechanism: the base stays generic, the .local carries the machine's specifics. The includeIf is the identity automation: any repo under ~/work/ gets the work email — the first work commit is correct without vigilance. The comment on gitconfig-work notes the judgment call: identity isn't secret, so it can be committed.

pitfalls: Single config everywhere — the work commit with the personal email; the second machine breaks the assumption.
Per-repo vigilance — the 'remember to set it' strategy; fails once, costs weeks.
Secrets in overrides committed — the .local with keys pushed; gitignore the secret-bearing layers.
No layering — the forked per-machine repos; the shared base rots separately.
lessons.try_it: Add the .local layer to one config and an includeIf git identity rule; verify with a test commit's author line.

lessons.title: Mastering the Command Palette
concepts: Palette as the interface: Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P — every command, fuzzy-searchable, one keystroke away.
Recent-first ranking: the frequent commands surface — the twice-daily hunt becomes 2 seconds.
Keybindings displayed: the palette teaches shortcuts — the head graduates to muscle memory.
Long-tail access: 500 commands, no memorization — the palette scales where binding doesn't.

example.code:
Try: Ctrl+Shift+P -> type 'fold all' -> Enter.
Notice: the keybinding shown beside it (learn it if daily).
> prefix: commands | @ prefix: symbols | # prefix: more.
The palette is also a calculator, a file finder, a settings search.
example.walkthrough: The try-it is the habit in miniature: invoke, fuzzy-type, notice the keybinding. The prefixes (>, @, #) reveal the palette as the multi-tool — commands, symbols, and more behind one keystroke. This is the workflow that retires the menu hunt permanently.

pitfalls: Menu-tree memorization — the five-level hunt; the palette inverts the search.
Binding everything — the 500-command fantasy; the palette owns the long tail.
Ignoring the displayed keybinding — the palette teaches; the graduation to muscle memory missed.
Palette as beginner tool — the power users live in it; the beginners live in menus.
lessons.try_it: For one day, reach every command via the palette — note which three deserve keybindings by day's end.

lessons.title: Multi-Cursor Power Editing
concepts: Ctrl/Cmd+D: next occurrence selected per press — incremental, visible, stoppable before false positives.
Alt+click: manual cursor placement — the irregular cases, the non-identical spots.
Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+L: all occurrences at once — the trusted-text rename in one keystroke.
Type once, edit N: the parallelism — each cursor live, every edit visible as it happens.

example.code:
Select a class name -> Ctrl+D (next occurrence) x11 -> type the new
name once. Watch all 12 change live.
Alt+click: place cursors on the irregular spots the text-select missed.
Esc: one cursor again. The dialog retires for the in-file case.
example.walkthrough: The walkthrough is the 20-second demo: select, grow the set with Ctrl+D, type once, watch. The Alt+click line covers the dialog's advantage (irregular spots) — multi-cursor handles those too, manually. The Esc is the exit — the skill includes knowing how to leave the mode.

pitfalls: Dialog-only editing — the serial fallback; the native parallelism ignored.
Replace All blindness — the false positive shipped; Ctrl+D's incremental growth prevents it.
One-by-one edits — the 12x chore; the cursors parallelize it.
Forgetting Esc — stranded in multi-cursor; the exit is part of the skill.
lessons.try_it: Rename one identifier across a file using only Ctrl+D and typing — then once more with Alt+click for irregular spots.

lessons.title: Rename Refactoring Across the Codebase
concepts: Shift+F6 rename: semantic symbol rename — declarations, references, imports via language analysis.
Preview before applying: the full occurrence list reviewed — the 40 files' changes, seen first.
Strings/comments opt-in: never silently renamed — the literal survives by default.
Atomic across files: one refactoring, all files — the rename as a single undoable unit.

example.code:
Place cursor on the class name -> Shift+F6 -> type new name.
Preview: the IDE lists every occurrence (40 files) — uncheck any
surprise. Strings/comments: separate checkboxes, default off.
Enter: all files updated atomically. The sed string-corruption: impossible.
example.walkthrough: The steps are the safety: cursor-on-symbol (the semantic anchor), preview (the 40 files seen), the unchecked surprise (the human override), atomic apply (the single undo). The string-corruption line is the sed failure made impossible — the default-off checkbox is the guard.

pitfalls: sed renames — the character-level rename; the string literal corrupted.
Blind apply — the preview skipped; the surprise occurrence shipped.
Manual 40-file rename — the human sed; the IDE's semantics are the tool.
Rename fear — the permanent bad name; the refactoring makes renames cheap.
lessons.try_it: Rename one real symbol with Shift+F6; read the full preview before applying — find one occurrence you didn't expect.

lessons.title: Structural Search and Replace
concepts: SSR templates: search the syntax tree (try/except/pass structure) — shape, not strings.
Placeholders ($stmts$): match any statements in the shape — the pattern generalizes.
Replace templates: rewrite all matches structurally — the 12 fixes, previewed, atomic.
Text search's successor: grep finds strings; SSR finds the code shapes grep can't express.

example.code:
Structural Search template:
  try:
    $stmts$
  except:
    pass
Matches: only the swallowing try/excepts (12 of 400 grep hits).
Replace template: except $e$: -> log + raise. Preview, apply.
example.walkthrough: The template is the query: the try/except/pass shape with $stmts$ as the wildcard. The 12-of-400 line is the precision payoff — the structural query vs the text query. The replace template shows the remediation at the same level: structural fix, previewed like the rename.

pitfalls: Regex heroics — the pattern that almost works; structure beats text.
Manual 400 — the diligence tax; the structural query is the tool.
No replace template — the 12 fixed by hand; the template applies the fix.
SSR ignorance — the IDE's most powerful search unused; the grep habit unexamined.
lessons.try_it: Write one SSR template for a code smell in your codebase; compare its hits to grep's.

lessons.title: Debugger Superpowers: Watches, Evaluate, and Breakpoint Conditions
concepts: Conditional breakpoints: pause on the failing case only — the 10,000 good requests skipped.
Evaluate Expression: run code in the paused frame — the 'what if' answered live.
Watches: track expressions across steps — the suspect under continuous observation.
Drop Frame: re-enter the method — retry with different inputs, no restart.

example.code:
Debug session:
1. Breakpoint with condition: user.id == 42 (the failing case only)
2. Pause -> Evaluate: user.getOrders().size() (the hypothesis, live)
3. Watch: total — step through, watch it go wrong
4. Drop Frame -> re-enter with fixed input. No restart, no prints.
example.walkthrough: The session is the workflow: condition (precision), evaluate (the live question), watch (the continuous eye), drop frame (the rewind). Each step replaces a print-restart cycle with a seconds-long interrogation. This is the debugger as the instrument it is — not the 'junior tool' of myth.

pitfalls: Print-restart loops — the hypothesis tax; the debugger answers live.
Unconditional breakpoints — the 10,000 pauses; conditions are the filter.
Debugger ignorance — the unused instrument; 'never learned it' was the bug.
No evaluate expression — the 'what if' unasked; the paused frame is a REPL.
lessons.try_it: Debug one real issue using only conditional breakpoints + Evaluate Expression — no new prints.

lessons.title: Attach to Process: Debugging the Unrestartable
concepts: Attach to Process: debugger joins the running service — no restart, no repro loss.
Matching PDBs: symbols must match the deployed binaries — the breakpoint-binding requirement.
Non-destructive: detach leaves it running — the investigation without the outage.
Code-type selection: managed/native/script — the debugger must speak the process's language.

example.code:
Debug > Attach to Process:
1. Find the service process (w3wp, yourservice.exe)
2. Attach to: Managed (.NET) / Native as appropriate
3. Verify symbols: Modules window -> Symbol Status = Loaded
4. Breakpoints bind (solid red). Investigate, then Detach All.
example.walkthrough: The steps are the ritual: find (the process), attach-type (the language), symbols (the binding proof), breakpoints (the investigation), detach (the clean exit). The Modules window check is the step everyone skips — the hollow breakpoint is the symptom of missing symbols, diagnosed here.

pitfalls: Restart-under-debugger — the dropped connections; the repro destroyed.
Hollow breakpoints ignored — the missing PDBs; the Modules window names them.
Wrong attach type — managed vs native mismatch; the debugger speaks the wrong language.
Kill-after-attach — the investigation ended with an outage; detach, don't terminate.
lessons.try_it: Attach to one running process (a local service); verify symbols load and a breakpoint binds.

lessons.title: MSBuild Diagnostics: The File the Compiler Can't See
concepts: Project file as the file list: Include/Condition — the compiler's world is the .csproj, not the disk.
Diagnostic verbosity: the real command lines — the file's absence from the invocation is the evidence.
Condition suspects: configuration/platform gates — the Debug-only file in Release.
Output window literacy: the real errors hide above the scroll — read the build, don't ritual it.

example.code:
Diagnosis:
1. Tools > Options > Build > verbosity: Diagnostic
2. Rebuild; search Output for the filename — absent from csc.exe args?
3. Check the .csproj: <Compile Include="..." /> present? Condition?
4. Found: Condition="'$(Configuration)'=='Debug'" on a Release build.
example.walkthrough: The steps are the elimination: verbosity (the evidence), the search (the absence proven), the project file (the suspect list), the condition (the culprit). The found line is the classic — the configuration-gated file, invisible in the other configuration. The ritual retires; the reading replaces it.

pitfalls: Clean-rebuild ritual — the sometimes-working magic; the log names the cause.
Disk-equals-project — the file 'exists' but isn't Included; the project file is the truth.
Normal verbosity — the command lines hidden; Diagnostic shows them.
bin/obj deletion as first resort — the shadow sometimes real, usually not; read first.
lessons.try_it: Set Diagnostic verbosity once; find one real command line in your next build and read what it includes.

lessons.title: Solution Configurations: Debug in Staging, Safely
concepts: RelWithDebInfo: optimized + symbols — production-like timing, debugger-capable.
Staging gets its own configuration: neither Debug nor Release — the instrumented faithful build.
Bounded logging: production levels in staging — the disk-filling debug spew prevented.
Fidelity first: investigate the system as it runs — the distorted twin hides Heisenbugs.

example.code:
Configuration Manager -> New: 'Staging' (copy from Release):
  Optimization: ON (timing faithful)
  Debug Info: Full PDBs (debugger + dumps work)
  Logging: production levels (disk safe)
Deploy Staging config to staging. Debug the real timing.
example.walkthrough: The new configuration is the practice: copied from Release (the fidelity), plus symbols (the instrument), minus the debug spew. The Configuration Manager step makes it a first-class build flavor — selectable, deployable, repeatable. The last line is the payoff: the debugger works AND the timing is real.

pitfalls: Debug builds in staging — the distorted twin; the timing-sensitive bug hides.
Unbounded debug logging — the filled disk; the investigation's collateral.
Release-without-symbols — the faithful but blind build; PDBs are the instrument.
Local-only reproduction — the staging-only bug exiled; the Staging config brings the debugger there.
lessons.try_it: Create a symbols-enabled Release-based configuration in one solution; verify the debugger attaches to it.

lessons.title: Reproducing the Unreproducible
concepts: Capture the habitat: inputs, state, timing, environment — the bug's context, preserved.
Delta-debug the trigger: halve until minimal — the 3-line repro from the 10,000-line log.
Automate the repro: script, then regression test — the fix verifiable, the return prevented.
Theories die fast: tested against the repro, not debated — the argument settled by evidence.

example.code:
Repro workflow:
1. Capture: the exact input + state + environment of a failure
2. Shrink: remove half the input — still fails? repeat. (delta debugging)
3. Script it: repro.sh / repro_test.py — one command, fails reliably
4. Fix, then run repro.sh — green. Keep it as the regression test.
example.walkthrough: The steps convert the Tuesday mystery into infrastructure: capture (the habitat), shrink (the minimal trigger), script (the automation), verify (the fix proven), keep (the regression guard). The repro.sh at the end is the artifact — the bug can never silently return, because its trigger is now a test.

pitfalls: Theory-first fixing — the unverifiable guess; the repro makes fixes provable.
Defensive tri-fix — the three theories all 'fixed'; the real one unknown.
No capture — the habitat lost; every session starts from zero.
Manual repro — the 20-step ritual; the script is the repro.
lessons.try_it: Take one flaky test or intermittent bug; shrink its trigger to the minimal case this week.

lessons.title: Binary Search Debugging: Halving the Suspects
concepts: Bisect the range: midpoint tested good/bad — logarithmic, not linear; ~8 tests for 300 commits.
git bisect: the bookkeeping automated — mark bad/good, test midpoints, the culprit emerges.
Fast good/bad test required: the repro script — the workflows compose; bisection needs the oracle.
Any ordered range: commits, configs, data — the halving works wherever 'when did it break' applies.

example.code:
git bisect start
 git bisect bad HEAD          # it breaks here
git bisect good v2.4.0        # it worked here
# bisect checks out the midpoint; you test and say:
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad
# ~8 rounds later: 'abc123 is the first bad commit' -> read ONE diff.
example.walkthrough: The session is the algorithm: bound the range (bad/good), test midpoints, halve. The 'read ONE diff' line is the payoff — the week's reading replaced by one diff review. The good/bad oracle is the prerequisite the repro lesson provides — the two workflows are one system.

pitfalls: Linear reading — the week's work; the logarithm is the tool.
No oracle — the good/bad test missing; bisection needs the repro script.
Biggest-commit blame — the astrology; the bisect is the measurement.
Skipping the bisect — the technique unknown; the most leveraged debugging skill unlearned.
lessons.try_it: Bisect one real regression (or simulate with a test repo); count your tests vs the commit count.

lessons.title: Reading Stack Traces Like a Map
concepts: Your frames first: the application code in the trace — the addresses, not the road.
Read the chain downward: who called whom into the failure — the guilty path, ordered.
Exception type + exact line: the what and the where — the diagnosis's two coordinates.
Framework frames as context: the road between your addresses — skimmed, not studied.

example.code:
Trace reading order:
  1. Scan for YOUR package frames (skip framework noise)
  2. Deepest YOUR frame = where your code entered the failure
  3. Read upward: the throw point (what failed)
  4. Read downward: the call chain (how it got there)
The 12-frames-down frame was the bug. Google never needed.
example.walkthrough: The numbered order is the technique: your frames (the filter), the deepest one (the entry), upward (the what), downward (the how). The framework-noise skip is the efficiency — 60 frames become the 5 that matter. The last line is the independence gained: the trace read well beats the search.

pitfalls: Top-line Googling — the stranger's bug fixed; your 12-frames-down bug unexamined.
Framework-frame fixation — the road studied; the addresses ignored.
Trace as noise — the 60 frames scrolled past; the map unread.
No line numbers noted — the where unrecorded; the diagnosis floats.
lessons.try_it: Take one real stack trace; write down the guilty chain (your frames only) before any searching.

lessons.title: Workspace vs User Settings: The Layering
concepts: User layer: personal (theme, keys) — machine-local, never committed.
Workspace layer: the team's contract (formatter, tabs, SDK) — committed, versioned with the code.
Contract travels with code: the checkout behaves correctly with zero setup — onboarding included.
No personal in shared: the 2-space tabs stay home — the formatting fight prevented by layering.

example.walkthrough: The JSON is the contract: tab size, format-on-save, the formatter identity, the interpreter path — the behaviors that must be identical everywhere. The ${workspaceFolder} variable keeps it portable — no hardcoded paths. The comment is the layering rule restated: personal stays in the user layer.

pitfalls: Personal in shared — the 2-space tabs in the repo; the PR fight.
Contract on one machine — CI formats differently; the workspace file missing.
No layers — the single file serving two audiences; the confusion structural.
Hardcoded paths — the teammate's machine breaks; variables keep it portable.
lessons.try_it: Split one settings file into user vs workspace layers; commit the workspace contract.

lessons.title: Vetting Extensions: Supply-Chain Safety
concepts: Publisher + permissions: verified identity, sane capabilities — the theme needs no network.
Update scrutiny: changelogs reviewed, versions pinned — the auto-update as the attack vector, contained.
Team allowlist: workspace recommended extensions — reviewed once, shared by all.
Extensions as dependencies: third-party code, first-party access — vetted like any dependency.

example.walkthrough: The extensions.json is the allowlist: recommendations (vetted, wanted) and unwantedRecommendations (the known-bad, blocked). The vetting comment is the process: publisher, permissions, update policy — per extension, once, shared. The version-pinning note contains the auto-update vector — the team's extensions update on review, not on release.

pitfalls: Popularity-as-vetting — the 2M installs; the victims counted, not the safety.
Auto-update everything — the exfil's delivery; pin and review.
Permission blindness — the theme with network access; the manifest unread.
No team list — every developer vets alone (or doesn't); the allowlist shares the work.
lessons.try_it: Audit your installed extensions: publisher, permissions, and why each is trusted — remove one you can't justify.

lessons.title: Settings Sync: Portable Environments
concepts: Settings Sync: keybindings, snippets, extensions, UI state — the new machine converges on sign-in.
Dotfiles for text forms: keybindings.json, snippets/ versioned — the diffable, historical record.
Setup as identity: any machine becomes yours — the laptop stops being special.
Extension list synced: the toolset travels — the new machine's IDE matches on day one.

example.code:
Portability checklist:
- Settings Sync ON (account-bound): keybindings, snippets, extensions, UI
- Dotfiles repo: keybindings.json, snippets/*.json (history + diff)
- extensions.json in repos: the project-relevant set
New machine: sign in -> converge -> code. The week retires.
example.walkthrough: The checklist is the two-layer practice: sync (the automatic convergence) plus dotfiles (the versioned text). The extensions.json line ties in the workspace lesson — the project layer joins the personal layers. The last line is the reclaimed week — the setup as a sign-in, not a project.

pitfalls: Hand reconfiguration — the week from memory; the sync is exact.
Laptop-local setup — the one perfect machine; the identity travels now.
Unsynced snippets — the best snippets stranded; the sync carries them.
Screenshot documentation — the pictures; the JSON is the artifact.
lessons.try_it: Enable Settings Sync today; verify a second machine (or fresh profile) converges to your setup.

lessons.title: The Integrated Terminal: Ending the Alt-Tab Loop
concepts: Integrated panels: split terminals for the long-runners — server, logs, shell, all in-editor.
Cwd follows the project: the terminal opens where the code is — the errand starts located.
Tasks for the frequent: test/build/lint as keystrokes — output in-panel, problems matched.
Zero switches: the 200 alt-tabs retired — the thread unbroken.

example.code:
Setup: Ctrl+` (integrated terminal) -> split: [npm run dev] [tail -f logs]
Bind tasks: Ctrl+Shift+B -> 'test' (output panel, problems parsed).
The loop: edit -> keystroke -> see results in-panel -> edit.
Alt-tab count today: zero.
example.walkthrough: The setup is the workflow: the keystroke opens the terminal where the code is, the splits hold the long-runners, the bound task runs the frequent command with parsed output. The loop line is the day: edit, keystroke, in-panel results, edit — no context leaves the editor. The zero at the end is the metric — count the alt-tabs, watch them vanish.

pitfalls: Alt-tab purism — the 200 daily switches; the thread dropped 200 times.
External terminal — the separate window; the integration unattempted.
Unbound commands — the frequent typed fully; the task keystroke unmade.
Single terminal panel — the long-runners fight; split them.
lessons.try_it: Move your three most-used terminal commands into the integrated terminal + one bound task today.

lessons.title: Shell Aliases and Functions: The Commands Everyone Retypes
concepts: Aliases for the constant: glog, gst — the 45 characters become 4; the typos vanish.
Functions for the parameterized: the shape constant, the argument varying — named and flexible.
Versioned in dotfiles: the set travels — the environment carries the shortcuts.
Named intent: the frequent command as vocabulary — the shell speaks your shorthand.

example.code:
# ~/.dotfiles/zsh/aliases.zsh (committed, synced)
alias glog='git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20'
alias gst='git status -sb'
gco() { git checkout "$1"; }   # parameterized: gco main
# 45 chars -> 4. Forty times a day. The typos: gone.
example.walkthrough: The aliases are the compression: the full commands named as intent. The function shows the parameterized case — the shape named, the argument passed. The committed path ties to the dotfiles practice: the shortcuts are environment, versioned and traveling. The arithmetic at the end is the justification — the daily savings, stated.

pitfalls: Full-command typing — the 45x40 ritual; the typo tax paid daily.
Unversioned aliases — the perfect set on one machine; the dotfiles carry them.
History-only retrieval — the past recalled; the frequent unnamed.
Cryptic names — the alias nobody remembers; memorable beats short.
lessons.try_it: Alias your five most-retyped commands today; commit them to the dotfiles.

lessons.title: Taming Build Output: Tasks with Problem Matchers
concepts: Tasks run the build: Ctrl+Shift+B — the build as a keystroke, output captured.
Problem matchers parse: file:line:column from compiler output — the text becomes entries.
Problems panel: the navigable list — click-to-jump, severity-sorted, the scroll retired.
Matcher per tool: tsc, eslint, gcc patterns — the format known, the parsing automatic.

example.walkthrough: The tasks.json is the practice: the label (the keystroke's target), the command, the $tsc matcher (the known format), the presentation (dedicated panel, silent unless errors). The comment flow is the day: keystroke, parse, panel, jump. The matcher is the hero — the compiler's format, understood.

pitfalls: Manual scrolling — the 400-line hunt, five times daily; the matcher navigates.
Unmatched tasks — the build runs, the output stays text; the matcher unconfigured.
grep navigation — the text found, the jump manual; the panel jumps.
No tasks — the build always in the raw terminal; the keystroke unbound.
lessons.try_it: Add one task with a problem matcher for your main build; use it instead of scrolling for a day.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: One technique per lesson: isolated, practiced same-day — the habit installed deliberately.
Exclusive week: use it for everything for a week — the default rewired, not just learned.
Layering: next technique on the solid previous — the twelve habits compound.
Hands, not eyes: the try-it is the lesson — reading about Ctrl+D builds nothing.

example.code:
Your setup: the IDE you actually use daily (this course meets you there),
a terminal, and one real project to practice on.
Pace: one lesson per day, try-it same day, exclusive-use week per
technique. The capstone assembles your environment at the end.
example.walkthrough: The setup meets the learner where they are — the daily IDE, not a mandated one — because habits form in the real workflow. The pace (one lesson/day, exclusive week) is the habit science: spaced, deliberate, layered. The capstone is the assembly — the twelve habits composed into one environment.

pitfalls: Tool collecting — the twelve extensions; the workflow unchanged.
Reading without doing — the theory-first plan; the hands unbuilt.
Skipped try-its — the lesson unread by the fingers; the habit uninstalled.
Technique hopping — the new trick daily; the myelination never completes.
lessons.try_it: Do lesson 1's try-it today — the habit program starts with the first technique.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: Muscle Memory Over Memorization
concepts: 3 at a time: the attention-sized set — learned, then automatic, then next.
Real work as practice: the pressure and context included — the habits pressure-tested.
Automaticity as the gate: used without thinking — the promotion criterion.
Menu vs meal: the sheet shows, the practice owns — memorization is the menu.

example.code:
Study loop per week: (1) pick 3 techniques from the course,
(2) use them exclusively in real work, (3) Friday check: used
without thinking? If yes, next 3. If no, another week.
The cheat sheet stays open — as the menu, not the meal.
example.walkthrough: The loop is the strategy operationalized: pick (the menu), exclusive use (the meal), Friday check (the gate). The 'another week' branch is the honesty — automaticity can't be rushed, and the loop respects that. The cheat sheet's role is explicit: reference, not curriculum.

pitfalls: List memorization — the 200 shortcuts; the fingers untrained.
Just-in-time learning — the moment's shortcut, Friday's forgetting.
Mouse fallback — the pressure default; the habits unbuilt.
No gate — the 'learned' untested; automaticity is the criterion.
lessons.try_it: Pick your first 3 techniques today; start the exclusive-use week now.

lessons.title: Course Map: The Fourteen Domains
concepts: Layered map: edit -> understand -> automate -> reproduce -> augment — the environment inside out.
Dependencies are the map: version what you've built; read before you automate.
AI on top: assistants augment solid fundamentals — the multiplier, not the foundation.
Capstone as assembly: the layers composed — your complete environment.

example.code:
The layers:
  EDIT: vscode, neovim, intellij-pycharm, visual-studio
  UNDERSTAND: debugging-workflows, profiling-perf, git-in-ide
  AUTOMATE: terminal-tasks, extensions-settings
  REPRODUCE: remote-devcontainers, dotfiles
  AUGMENT: ai-coding-assistants
Every lesson: which layer am I in, what does it serve?
example.walkthrough: The layer diagram is the orienting habit — asked at every lesson, the fourteen domains stay one environment. The 'which layer, what does it serve' question keeps the architecture live: the profiling lesson serves debugging, the dotfiles lesson serves everything. AI's placement (augment, last) is the course's thesis: the multiplier on fundamentals, not a substitute.

pitfalls: Tip collections — the fourteen lists; the environment view is the curriculum.
AI-first ordering — the multiplier before the fundamentals; the foundation first.
Skipping to 'interesting' domains — containers before editing skill; the layers punish reordering.
No capstone — the environment never assembled; the composition unproven.
lessons.try_it: Draw the layer diagram from memory; place each domain you've studied — the map check.

lessons.title: Assessment Strategy: Proving Tooling Fluency
concepts: Capstone demoed live: the environment at speed — the fluency visible, not described.
Habit record: twelve techniques automatic — the pressure-proofing documented.
Scenarios as narratives: 'when I...' workflow stories — the interview answers pre-lived.
Honest framing: no certificate, no affiliation — the demonstrated fluency is the credential.

example.code:
Interview prep: (1) capstone environment demo-ready (navigate, debug,
profile live), (2) five scenario narratives as 'tell me about a time'
answers, (3) the technique catalog fluent under pressure,
(4) one timed exercise: the habit record proves the speed.
The watcher sees the hands.
example.walkthrough: The four prep items map to the watched interview: the demo (the fluency), the narratives (the judgment), the catalog (the breadth), the timed exercise (the proof under pressure). The 'watcher sees the hands' line is the preparation's thesis — every item is performative, not declarative.

pitfalls: Vocabulary prep — the named refactorings; the watched hands unfluent.
Q&A memorization — the answers recited; the pairing session exposes.
No demo ready — 'show me your setup' with nothing to show; the capstone is the show.
Claiming certification — the honest framing is the trust asset; never claim it.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: Designing Your Environment
concepts: Layered design: edit/understand/automate/reproduce/augment — the course map, personalized.
Choices with reasons: the design doc — the rationale the interview probes.
Design before build: the doc reviewed first — the junk drawer prevented.
Your environment, not theirs: the copied dotfiles skipped the decisions — decide.

example.code:
Design doc (1 page): per layer, the tools chosen + why.
Edit: Neovim (init.lua) for code, VS Code for debugging.

example.walkthrough: The one-page doc is the environment's blueprint: each layer's choices, each choice's reason. The example shows the personalization — two editors, each for its strength, the reasons stated. The doc is also the demo's script: the capstone presentation walks the layers.

pitfalls: Tool pile — the junk drawer; the undesigned accumulation.
Copied dotfiles — the decisions skipped; the interview probes them.
No doc — the rationale unrecorded; the design unreviewable.
One layer only — the editor configured, the rest default; the layers compose.

lessons.title: Capstone Build: Assembling the Layers
concepts: Every layer built: configs, tasks, aliases, containers, dotfiles, AI brief — the doc made real.
Verified per layer: each lesson's criteria — the try-its as acceptance tests.
Bootstrap test: fresh VM to full environment — the reproduction proven, not claimed.
Fluency over intentions: the demo shows the working environment — the build, not the doc.

pitfalls: Doc-only capstone — the beautiful intentions; the environment defaults.

Unverified layers — the 'done' unclaimed; the try-its are the tests.
No bootstrap test — the reproduction claimed; the VM proves it.

concepts: Recorded tour: the layers at speed — the watchable fluency, the interview artifact.

Repos linked: dotfiles, devcontainer — the artifacts, inspectable.
